## keyframeCodeBlend.kt { #keyframecodeblend-kt }

Blending two *code* keyframes by finding the structure they share and interpolating the numbers
they do not.

A [`KeyframeScope`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keyframescope) can snapshot code as well as values: a `stack.auto` StackSL program through
`KeyframeScope.stackAuto`, and a Kotlin expression through the `sourceBlock { }` macro. Two such
snapshots have no midpoint in general — half a program is not a program — so
`KeyframeScope.interpolate` steps them, taking the right-hand source once `t >= 1`. That is all
that is available when the two programs disagree about what they do.

When they *agree* about what they do and differ only in numbers, there is a real midpoint, and
this file finds it. Both sources are lexed, the two token streams are aligned, and every place
where the alignment pairs a number with a number becomes a [`CodeBlendSite`](graphics.md#keyframecodeblend-kt-codeblendsite). Anything the
alignment cannot pair is a [`CodeBlendDivergence`](graphics.md#keyframecodeblend-kt-codeblenddivergence), and one divergence is enough to put the whole
slot back on the stepping path: a program built from the left structure with the right numbers,
where the two structures differ, is neither keyframe at either end.

### The two ways to spend the blend

`CodeBlendMode.STATIC` writes the interpolated numbers into the source and hands back a new
program, which the slot then compiles. It reaches every site — including StackSL's modifier chains
and random ranges, whose grammar demands literals — and it costs a shader compile (or, for Kotlin,
a K2 compile) per value of `t`. Scrubbing a timeline or stepping between two looks is what it is
for; sixty times a second is not.

`CodeBlendMode.RUNTIME` emits *one* program in which each moving site reads the blend from
outside. The program is then invariant in `t`, so it compiles once and animates for free. StackSL
gets there by rewriting `0.5` as `0.2 0.9 ?pc.keyframeBlend .x mix` — a push of each endpoint and
the builtin `mix`, which leaves one value on the stack exactly as the literal it replaced did, so
the surrounding stack arithmetic is untouched. Kotlin gets there by rewriting `0.5f` as
`afield.animation.keyframes.kfMix(0.2f, 0.9f, ...)`. Sites a mix expression cannot reach — see
`StackSLNumericFormKind` — make the plan report `CodeBlendPlan.runtimeCapable` false, and a
RUNTIME request over one of those falls back to STATIC and says so.

### The push-constant convention

A StackSL program can only read what the host has already put in the shader, and a `stack.auto`
slot cannot declare a uniform of its own. So the blend parameter arrives by convention: declare a
`vec4` called `keyframeBlend` in the shader's push-constant block, and register the matching
keyframe lane so the scope can write it.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
layout(push_constant) uniform Controls {
    vec4 keyframeBlend;
} pc;
```
```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
scope.target("keyframeBlend") { module.current.liveUniformStructures["pc"] }
scope.codeBlend = CodeBlendOptions(mode = CodeBlendMode.RUNTIME)
```

`KeyframeScope.interpolate` then fills that lane with `keyframeBlendVector` on every blend, and
the four components are four shapes of the same parameter — see [`CodeBlendLane`](graphics.md#keyframecodeblend-kt-codeblendlane). A vec4 rather
than a float because a push-constant block is padded to vec4 boundaries anyway, and because a
program that wants the eased blend for one number and the raw one for another should not need a
second uniform to say so.

The names are defaults (`keyframeBlendPushConstant`, `keyframeBlendKey`); a shader whose block
instance is called something other than `pc` sets `CodeBlendOptions.stackSLRead` to match.

## keyframeSweep.kt { #keyframesweep-kt }

Overnight exploration of a keyframe space: a directory of saved keys in, an archive of renders out.

A [`KeyframeScope`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keyframescope) gives you one look at a time — capture it, edit it, put it back. A directory of
saved keys is something else: a *space*, whose interesting points are mostly the ones nobody has
visited. [`KeyframeSweep`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt-keyframesweep) visits them while you sleep. Each pass draws a few keys from the pool,
blends them at random weights (sometimes past either end of the hull), applies the blend to the
live scope, makes a directory, and hands that directory to a `suspend` callback of yours which
runs to completion before the next pass starts. What the callback writes there is its business —
a still, a clip, a mesh, a CSV. What the sweep writes there is the provenance: the blended key as
ordinary key JSON, and a manifest saying which keys went in at which weights.

The point of the archive is what happens to it afterwards. A night of this is a few thousand
directories to categorise, cluster, score or hand to a model, and the sweep's job is to make that
second pass possible: every render is self-describing, `index.jsonl` is one line per render for a
reader that does not want to walk the tree, and `renders/` is itself a valid keyframe pool — so
tonight's output is a legitimate input for tomorrow night.

### The blend is a fold, not new maths

`KeyframeScope.interpolate` already knows how every lane type blends — numbers and vectors lerp,
quaternions slerp, `CameraPose` sclerp, code blends or steps. So an N-way blend here is a
*pairwise fold* over it rather than a second type table that would immediately drift from the
first: with weights sorted descending and running sums `S`, folding `t = w / S` at each step
yields exactly the affine weighted mean for every linear lane, and inherits the rest for free.

Sorting descending is what makes it safe rather than merely neat. Weights sum to 1, so the running
sums start at the largest weight and end at 1, rising while the terms are positive and falling
once they go negative — the minimum is therefore `min(w_max, 1)`, which is always positive. No
division ever approaches zero, including under extrapolation, where some weights *are* negative.

Three things the fold alone gets wrong, and this file handles on purpose — see [`DiscreteBlend`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt-discreteblend),
[`MissingSlots`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt-missingslots) and `SweepConfig.preserveNumericKind`. All three are recorded per render rather
than assumed, because an archive you cannot interrogate later is a wasted night.

### What a night survives

Nothing here trusts the run to finish. A render's manifest is written *before* its callback and
rewritten after, atomically, so a crashed pass is identifiable as one; `SweepConfig.resume` picks
up where the process died and re-derives each render's randomness from `seed + index`, so skipping
completed work cannot change what the unfinished work would have drawn. A throwing callback is
one failed render, not a lost night — until `SweepConfig.maxConsecutiveFailures` of them in a row
says the night is broken. And `SweepConfig.minFreeBytes` stops the sweep before the disk does.

Every knob a sweep has, as one serializable value — so the run's own configuration is recorded in `sweep.json` beside its output and a night is reproducible from its archive rather than from whatever the box said at the time.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">seed</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span></code> | Root of the run's randomness. Every render draws from `seed` and its own index, nothing else. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">count</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | How many renders to attempt. Left unbounded, `maxDurationMs` or the disk floor ends the run. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">pattern</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | Which files under the pool directory are keys. See `everyKeyGlob`, and `keyFilesMatching`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">minArity</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Fewest keys in one blend. `1` is meaningful and worth allowing: a blend of one key is that key replayed exactly, which salts the archive with unmixed references to compare the blends against. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maxArity</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Most keys in one blend, clamped to the pool size. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">concentration</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | The Dirichlet concentration the weights are drawn from, and the single most consequential number here. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">extrapolationProbability</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | How often a blend is pushed outside the hull of its participants. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">minExtrapolationGain</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Least push, measured in hull-crossings from the anchor. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maxExtrapolationGain</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Most push. Past about `3.0` most looks fall apart, which is occasionally the point. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">discrete</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DiscreteBlend</span></code> | See [`DiscreteBlend`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt-discreteblend). |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">missingSlots</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MissingSlots</span></code> | See [`MissingSlots`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt-missingslots). |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">preserveNumericKind</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Round each blended number back to the numeric type the anchor held it in. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">applyToScope</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Write the blend to the live scope before calling the callback. Off makes the sweep a pure generator. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">restoreScopeAtEnd</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Put the scope back the way it was found when the run ends, however it ends. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maxDurationMs</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span></code> | Wall-clock budget in milliseconds; `0` for none. The "stop at 7am" knob. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">minFreeBytes</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span></code> | Stop while this many bytes are still free on the archive's filesystem. Eight gigabytes by default, which is generous on purpose: an overnight sweep of GPU stills is a *rate* of disk consumption, and the thing that goes wrong is not the archive being large but the machine having nothing left at 4am. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maxConsecutiveFailures</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Consecutive failures that mean the night is broken rather than the render unlucky. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">resume</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Skip renders a previous process already finished. See `KeyframeSweep.run`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">keepFailedRenders</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Keep the directory of a failed render, with its manifest and partial output, for forensics. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">arity</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">IntRange</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframeSweep/#L351) | `minArity``..``maxArity`, for reading. |

| Declaration | Summary |

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">format</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> |  |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">index</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> |  |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">id</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> |  |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">seed</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span></code> | The per-render seed, derived from `SweepConfig.seed` and `index`. Redraws this render exactly. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">status</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | `running`, `ok`, `failed` or `cancelled`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">startedAt</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> |  |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">finishedAt</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> |  |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">durationMs</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span><span class="o">?</span></code> |  |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">parents</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">SweepParent</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | The keys that went in, and at what weight. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">anchor</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | The parent that won the discrete lanes, and supplies numeric types under `preserveNumericKind` — drawn by roulette over the final weights, so it is usually the key that dominates the picture. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">extrapolationPole</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | The parent this blend was pushed *away* from, for an extrapolated render — a different key from `anchor`, and deliberately so: the earliest version of this gave one key both jobs, and produced blends wearing the palette of the look they had just fled. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">extrapolationGain</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | How far outside the hull this blend sits, in hull-crossings from the anchor — `1.0` is exactly on the far face, `1.5` is half as far again beyond it. ## keyframeSweepCapture.kt { #keyframesweepcapture-kt }

The GPU half of a keyframe sweep: turning one blended look into the still and the short clip that
a night's archive is actually made of.

[`KeyframeSweep`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt-keyframesweep) is renderer-free on purpose — it blends, it records, it calls your callback. But
*most* callbacks do the same two things, and they are the two things with traps in them: an
offscreen readback that can come back empty, and a frame sequence that has to be muxed by a tool
which may not be installed. So they live here once rather than in every sweep.

Both helpers follow the pattern the RectSL and StackSL gallery harnesses established: **one**
renderer and one `RenderToTexture` for the whole run, reused across thousands of renders, with
only the uniforms changing. Building a target per render is what makes an overnight sweep run out
of device memory at 3am.

Neither helper will invent a file. A readback that comes back empty and a missing `ffmpeg` are
both recorded as an artifact with a null path and a stated reason, and the frame PNGs are left on
disk so the clip can be muxed later. An archive that says what it is missing can be analysed; one
with a plausible-looking wrong file in it cannot.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframeSweepCapture.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframeSweepCapture/)

**Used in:** [Sweeping saved keyframes overnight](../keyframe_autosweep.md)

## keyframer.kt { #keyframer-kt }

Snapshot, interpolate and persist the live state of a running sketch. A [`KeyframeScope`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keyframescope) is a set
of named targets — typed Kotlin locals, keyframe-aware `controlGroup` controls, contributors such
as a score object, uniform `Structure` bindings, the uniform structures of a `ModulePointer` /
`ComputeModulePointer` / `MeshModulePointer`, a stackAuto shader-source slot via
`KeyframeScope.stackAuto`, or a `Camera` pose via `KeyframeScope.camera`. `capture()` reads them
all into a `KeyframeScope.Key`; invoking that `Key` writes them all back.

`KeyframeScope.interpolate` blends two keys per value type: numbers and vectors lerp, quaternions
slerp, dual quaternions and `CameraPose` sclerp, and strings / [`StackSLString`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-stackslstring) /
`SourceBackedBlock` step to the right-hand value at `t >= 1`. `remap` can re-time an individual
key's `t`. The two code types can do better than stepping when the two sources differ only in
numbers — see `KeyframeScope.codeBlend` and `keyframeCodeBlend.kt`.

Persistence goes through the [`KValue`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-kvalue) serial union, so only the types `KValue.fromAny` recognises
survive a save — numbers, vec2/3/4, quaternion, dual quaternion, camera pose, string, StackSL
source and source-backed block; anything else is silently dropped. Every `saveKey` also writes a
numbered copy into a `<file>.versions` directory with a manifest, which
`KeyframeScope.keyVersions` lists and `KeyframeScope.loadLatestKey` follows. `KeyframeScope.missingKey` supplies defaults for
keys absent from an older file, optionally per schema version.

Keys render themselves as HTML for box output ([`KeyDiff`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keydiff), `diffHtml`), and
`copyUpdateCodeToClipboard` emits pasteable Kotlin — that one goes through the AWT clipboard.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/)

**Used in:** [Keyframes: capturing, persisting and replaying live state](../keyframer_examples.md), [Values over time: interpolants & keyframes](../interpolants_examples.md)

### NumKind { #keyframer-kt-numkind }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">NumKind</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L164)

Which Kotlin numeric type a saved number came from, so that `KValue.toAny` can hand back a `Byte`/`Short`/`Int`/`Long`/`Float`/`Double` rather than always a `Double` — a uniform bound to an `Int` has to come back as an `Int`.

Constants: `BYTE`, `SHORT`, `INT`, `LONG`, `FLOAT`, `DOUBLE`.

### KValue { #keyframer-kt-kvalue }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">sealed</span> <span class="k">interface</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L185)

The closed set of value types a `KeyframeScope.Key` can *persist*: numbers, vec2/3/4, quaternion, dual quaternion, camera pose, string, StackSL source and source-backed block. A key in memory holds plain Kotlin values; this is the serial union they are converted to on the way to disk and back.

| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">SourceBlock</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">boxId</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">source</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L257) | A `SourceBackedBlock` reduced to the box it came from and its Kotlin source — the *live lambda* is not persisted. | [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">toAny</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Any</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L266) | Rebuild the live Kotlin value this entry stands for — the load half of the round trip. A [`DualQuat`](math.md#linalg-kt-dualquat) and a `CameraPoseValue` are re-normalised on the way out, because a rigid transform that has drifted is a broken transform; a plain [`Quat`](math.md#linalg-kt-quat) is **not** (see its own note — it may be standing in for something that is not a rotation). Numbers regain their [`NumKind`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-numkind) type, and a `SourceBlock` becomes a `SourceBackedBlock` that has not compiled anything yet. |

### KeyDTO { #keyframer-kt-keydto }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">KeyDTO</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">schemaVersion</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Map</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L355)

What a saved key looks like on disk: a schema version and a name → [`KValue`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-kvalue) map, pretty-printed as JSON with `type` as the discriminator.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">schemaVersion</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | The owning scope's `schemaVersion` at the moment of saving. Nothing validates it on load: a mismatch is not an error, it only selects which `KeyframeScope.missingKey` defaults apply. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Map</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | The key's entries by name. Values that `KValue.fromAny` could not represent are already gone. |

### KeyVersionInfo { #keyframer-kt-keyversioninfo }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">KeyVersionInfo</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">index</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">timestamp</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">note</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">file</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L374)

One row of a key file's version history, as recorded in the `<file>.versions/manifest.json` that every `saveKey` appends to. `KeyframeScope.keyVersions` hands these back, sorted by `index`.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">index</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Monotonic version number, starting at 0 and simply "highest so far plus one" — a save counter, not a schema version and not related to `KeyDTO.schemaVersion`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">timestamp</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | When the version was written, as an ISO-8601 `Instant.now()` string in UTC — or, for a row rebuilt from the file alone, that file's last-modified time. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">note</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Whatever note was passed to `saveKey`, for telling two snapshots apart later. A row rebuilt from the file alone says `"(recovered from disk; the manifest row for this version was lost)"` here instead, since the real note lived only in the manifest that went missing. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">file</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | File name inside the `.versions` directory, `"%06d.json"` of `index`. |

### KeyframeScope { #keyframer-kt-keyframescope }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">KeyframeScope</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">schemaVersion</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L444)

A named set of live things worth snapshotting — uniform `Structure` bindings, a module's live uniforms, a `stack.auto` shader slot, a `Camera` — plus the machinery to capture, blend, save and reload them. This is the object you keep around for the lifetime of a sketch.

| --- | --- |

| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">remap</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L472) | Per-key re-timing for `interpolate`: `remap["gain"] = { t -> t * t * (3 - 2 * t) }` eases that one value on a smoothstep while everything else stays linear. |

Get one from `capture`, `interpolate`, `loadKey`, or by constructing it from a map you wrote by hand (as the docs examples do). |

### KeyDiffKind { #keyframer-kt-keydiffkind }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">KeyDiffKind</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L1584)

How one name differs between two keys, always read left-to-right: `ADDED` means the right key has it and the left does not, `REMOVED` the other way round, `CHANGED` that both have it with unequal values. There is no "same" kind — unchanged names are left out of a diff entirely.

Constants: `ADDED`, `REMOVED`, `CHANGED`.

### KeyDiffEntry { #keyframer-kt-keydiffentry }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">KeyDiffEntry</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">kind</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KeyDiffKind</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">left</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Any</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">right</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Any</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L1587)

One line of a [`KeyDiff`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keydiff): what the name was on each side, and which way it moved.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | The key name, as it appears in both snapshots (`@`-qualified if that is how it was registered). |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">kind</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KeyDiffKind</span></code> | Whether this name was added, removed, or changed between left and right. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">left</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Any</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | The left-hand value; null for an `ADDED` entry, which had none. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">right</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Any</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | The right-hand value; null for a `REMOVED` entry. |

### KeyDiff { #keyframer-kt-keydiff }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">KeyDiff</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">leftName</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">rightName</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">entries</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">KeyDiffEntry</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ToHTML</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L1617)

The difference between two `KeyframeScope.Key`s: only the names that actually moved, sorted by name, ready to render. Produced by `Key.diff`.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">leftName</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | Heading for the left-hand column — cosmetic, defaulting to `"left"` at the call site. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">rightName</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | Heading for the right-hand column. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">entries</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">KeyDiffEntry</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | The changes, name-sorted; empty means the two keys agree. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">override</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">toString</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L1629) | The diff as text, one line per change prefixed `+` (added), `-` (removed) or `~` (changed), and the single line "No key differences." when there are none. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">override</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">toHTML</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L1644) | The diff as a small dark-mode HTML table — one row per change, marker coloured green for added, red for removed and amber for changed, with a header counting the changes. ## fline_graph_connectivity.kt { #fline-graph-connectivity-kt }

Bridge from drawn geometry to the graph algorithms: turns one or more `FLine`s into a welded
point graph.

`flineGraph`, or the `toFLineGraph` extensions on `FLine` and `Iterable<FLine>`, adaptively
subdivides cubics down to `cubicFlatness`, samples every node, then welds samples closer than
`epsilon` using a uniform grid plus union-find (`epsilon = 0` welds only bit-identical
positions). A welded vertex is the mean of the samples that reached it, and
`FLineGraph.vertexSources` records which line index and node instruction each of those samples
came from. Edges join consecutive samples, `close()` joins back to the subpath start,
self-edges are dropped and duplicates collapse to the shortest.

The result carries a `PointGraph` of `GraphEdge`s — the same types as `graph_connectivity.kt` —
so the search, spanning-tree and analysis functions there apply directly to a drawing.

## graph_connectivity.kt { #graph-connectivity-kt }

Self-contained graph / computational-geometry library over 2D and 3D point sets
(`Vec2`/`Vec3`). Every algorithm has a `vec2*` and (where meaningful) a `vec3*` entry point
returning a [`PointGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt-pointgraph); see each function's own KDoc for its definition and complexity.

Proximity / neighbourhood families: KNN (`vec2KnnGraph`), Orthant (`vec2OrthantGraph`),
Relative Neighborhood (`vec2RelativeNeighborhoodGraph`), Gabriel (`vec2GabrielGraph`),
Beta-Skeleton (`vec2BetaSkeleton`), Nearest-Neighbor (`vec2NearestNeighborGraph`),
Minimum Spanning Tree (`vec2MinimumSpanningTree`), Maximum-Diameter/radius
(`vec2MaximumDiameterGraph`), Maximum-Cut (`vec2MaximumCutGraph`) and Complete
(`vec2CompleteGraph`) graphs.

JTS-backed (2D only): full Delaunay triangulation (`vec2DelaunayGraph`, `vec2DelaunayTriangles`),
Urquhart (`vec2UrquhartGraph`, a real Urquhart graph built by removing the longest edge of each
Delaunay triangle — the 3D `vec3UrquhartGraph` is an MST approximation because Field only wires
2D Delaunay), Voronoi diagram/dual (`vec2VoronoiDiagram`, `vec2VoronoiDualGraph`) and convex
hull (`vec2ConvexHull`, `vec2ConvexHullGraph`, `vec2HullProjectionGraph`).

Traversal / analysis: BFS/DFS/A* path search, [`GraphEdgeVisitState`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt-graphedgevisitstate) greedy walks and
graph-diameter path decomposition (see the search/path functions below), plus FLine rendering
integration in `fline_graph_connectivity.kt`.

Custom distance metrics: pass `GraphConnectivityOptions.customDistanceMetric`. It is honoured by
the distance-driven algorithms (KNN, MST, RNG, Gabriel, Beta-Skeleton, Delaunay/Urquhart edge
weights, etc.). This includes `vec2OrthantGraph`/`vec3OrthantGraph`, whose nearest-neighbour
ranking within each orthant honours `customDistanceMetric` when supplied (Euclidean otherwise).

Smoke tests: `afield.examples.stdlib.GraphConnectivitySmokeTest` (its `runTests()` drives 35
checks, covering path search, edge-visit-state and FLine rendering as well as the core graphs).
Live rendered examples: `public/docs/graph_connectivity_examples.md`.

## mesh.kt { #mesh-kt }

[`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) — the CPU triangle mesh Field's 3D geometry family is built on, plus the builder that
makes one and the whole-mesh transforms that move one around.

A [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) is *not* a renderer buffer (that is Field 4's
[`afield.graphics.render.Mesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-src-jvmmain-kotlin-afield-graphics-render-mesh)) and *not* a graph of vertex objects. It is flat
`FloatArray` attribute storage plus an `IntArray` of triangle indices: the layout every algorithm
in this family wants, the layout a GPU upload wants, and cheap to copy. Positions are required;
normals, uvs and per-vertex colours are optional and either absent or complete.

The reason the vertices are floats-in-an-array rather than `List<Vec3>` is that `Vec3` is a
*mutable* `Vector3f`. A mesh holding shared mutable vectors is a mesh where `mesh.position(0).y +=
1` silently edits the mesh — or worse, edits three triangles because the vector was shared. So
every accessor here (`position`, `normal`, `uv`, `color`) returns a **fresh** vector you own, and
the `…Into` variants let a hot loop reuse one.

### The family

| file | what it adds |
|---|---|
| `mesh.kt` | this: the type, [`TriMeshBuilder`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimeshbuilder) / `triMesh`, transforms, concatenation |
| `mesh_topology.kt` | [`MeshTopology`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt-meshtopology) — adjacency, boundary loops, components, manifoldness, Euler characteristic / genus, `TriMesh.weld`, `TriMesh.fixWinding` |
| `mesh_generate.kt` | `boxMesh`, `uvSphereMesh`, `icosphereMesh`, `torusMesh`, `cylinderMesh`, `extrudeMesh`, `revolveMesh`, `tubeMesh`, `heightfieldMesh`, `reliefMesh` |
| `mesh_sdf.kt` | [`ScalarField3D`](graphics.md#mesh-sdf-kt-scalarfield3d), the SDF primitives / combinators, and `marchingCubes` |
| `mesh_process.kt` | `TriMesh.loopSubdivide`, `TriMesh.laplacianSmooth`, `TriMesh.taubinSmooth`, `TriMesh.withVertexNormals`, `TriMesh.decimate` |
| `mesh_measure.kt` | `TriMesh.surfaceArea`, `TriMesh.signedVolume`, curvature, [`MeshBvh`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt-meshbvh) (rays, closest point, inside test) |
| `mesh_io.kt` | OBJ and STL, read and write |
| `mesh_field.kt` | the bridges: `TriMesh.toFLines`, `VoronoiCell3.toTriMesh`, `Box.showMesh` |

### Conventions

- **Winding is counter-clockwise seen from outside**, so `faceNormal` points out of a closed
  solid and `signedVolume` of one is positive. Everything in the family agrees on this, and
  `TriMesh.fixWinding` repairs a mesh that does not.
- Nothing here mutates: every operation returns a new [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh). The arrays are `val`s and are
  not copied on construction, so do not hand a builder's scratch array to the constructor and
  then keep writing to it — use `TriMeshBuilder.build`.
- No dependencies beyond the Kotlin stdlib and Field's own generated linalg. No GPU, no AWT, no
  model-format libraries.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val ball = icosphereMesh(subdivisions = 3, radius = 1.0)
val shell = ball.scaled(1.0, 0.6, 1.0).withVertexNormals()
println("${shell.triangleCount} tris, volume ${shell.signedVolume()}")
display(shell.toFLines())            // draw its wireframe
```

## mesh_field.kt { #mesh-field-kt }

What makes the mesh family *Field's* rather than a generic geometry library: the bridges out of
[`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) and into the things Field already draws, renders and displays.

Four bridges:

 1. **Mesh → [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline).** `TriMesh.toFLines` gives you the wireframe, the silhouette-free edge set,
    the open boundary loops or the normals as drawable lines, so a marched iso-surface goes
    straight into the same drawing / animation / export machinery as anything hand-drawn — and is
    visible in a Field document *today*, with no renderer set up.
 2. **Mesh → pixels.** `TriMesh.renderPng` rasterises the mesh — perspective, z-buffer,
    perspective-correct attributes, two-light lambert, depth-tested wireframe — by packing it for
    `VisionGeometryPreview`'s renderer, which already had all of that. `Box.showMesh` pushes the
    result to a box output and `TriMesh.toHTML` uses it for the inline value thumbnail, so
    evaluating a mesh in a box shows the shape.
 3. **3D Voronoi → mesh.** `VoronoiCell3.toTriMesh` and `VoronoiLattice.toTriMesh` triangulate the
    polygonal cells `voronoi.kt` already computes by half-space clipping. Field could compute a 3D
    Voronoi diagram and not turn it into geometry; now it can.
 4. **Field lines → mesh.** `tubeMesh` on an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline), so a drawn stroke becomes a solid.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val cells = voronoi3d(List(24) { vec(rand(-1, 1), rand(-1, 1), rand(-1, 1)) })
val solid = cells.toTriMesh(shrink = 0.9)   // every cell, shrunk toward its own site
showMesh(solid, caption = "${solid.triangleCount} triangles from 24 sites")
```

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_field.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_field/)

**Used in:** [Geometry from disk](../geometry_from_disk.md), [Meshes and 3D geometry](../mesh_examples.md), [Three.js scenes with `three { … }`](../three_output.md)

| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">yawDegrees</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Orbit around `+y`, in degrees. `0` looks straight down `-z`. |

## mesh_generate.kt { #mesh-generate-kt }

Where a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) comes from: the primitives (`boxMesh`, `uvSphereMesh`, `icosphereMesh`,
`torusMesh`, `cylinderMesh`, `coneMesh`, `capsuleMesh`, the five platonics) and the *derived*
generators that build one out of something you already have (`extrudeMesh`, `revolveMesh`,
`tubeMesh`, `heightfieldMesh`, `reliefMesh`, `polygonMesh`).

### Welding and normals

**Everything here is welded and watertight where it can be.** A generator returns the minimal
vertex set, so `MeshTopology.eulerCharacteristic` of a box, a sphere, a cone or a capped cylinder
is exactly `2`, of a torus exactly `0`, and `TriMesh.isWatertight` is true. The volume, curvature
and decimation code all need that; a mesh that merely renders is not enough for any of them.

**Normals are only attached where they are unambiguous.** A sphere, icosphere, torus and capsule
are smooth everywhere, so they carry per-vertex normals. A box, cylinder, cone, extrusion or
platonic solid has *creases*: the two faces meeting at an edge want different normals at the same
vertex, and you cannot have both a shared vertex and two normals. Duplicating the vertex would
break watertightness and averaging across the crease would round it off, so these ship with
**no** normals and you pick:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
boxMesh().flatShaded()          // one normal per triangle: hard edges, 3 verts per tri
boxMesh().shadedNormals(35.0)   // split only where faces disagree by > 35 degrees
boxMesh().withVertexNormals()   // one averaged normal per shared vertex: rounded corners
```

The preview / render bridges in `mesh_field.kt` call `TriMesh.shadedNormals` for you when a mesh
arrives without normals, so a bare `boxMesh()` still looks like a box.

### Orientation

`+y` is up, matching the preview camera. Radial generators sweep `x = r cos u, z = -r sin u`, which
is the handedness that makes counter-clockwise-from-outside windings come out right. `planeMesh`
and `polygonMesh` live in the `xy` plane facing `+z`; `heightfieldMesh` lives in the `xz` plane
facing `+y`: a plane is a wall and a heightfield is a landscape.

## mesh_io.kt { #mesh-io-kt }

Getting a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) in and out of the two formats every 3D tool on the machine can already read:
**OBJ** (text, indexed, carries normals and uvs) and **STL** (ASCII or binary, triangle soup, the
lingua franca of 3D printing).

Both directions, in pure Kotlin, and what each format carries is different:

 - `TriMesh.toObj` / `objToTriMesh` keep the index structure, so a watertight mesh round-trips as a
   watertight mesh. Normals and uvs survive; per-vertex colours do not (OBJ has no standard for
   them). Faces with more than three corners are fan-triangulated on read, so a quad-mesh OBJ from
   a modeller loads fine.
 - `TriMesh.toStlAscii` / `TriMesh.toStlBinary` / `stlToTriMesh` are *triangle soup*, because STL
   has no vertex sharing at all: a mesh written to STL and read back has `3 * triangleCount`
   vertices and reports every edge as a boundary. `stlToTriMesh(bytes).weld()` gives you the mesh
   back. The read path does not weld for you, because welding needs a tolerance, and a tolerance
   guessed on your behalf is what loses a hairline feature.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val mesh = icosphereMesh(3)
File("/tmp/ball.obj").writeText(mesh.toObj())
File("/tmp/ball.stl").writeBytes(mesh.toStlBinary())
val back = objToTriMesh(File("/tmp/ball.obj").readText())
```

These two formats, and no others — see `meshFromFile` for where to go for PLY, glTF and GLB, and
`public/docs/geometry_from_disk.md` for the measured account of what each format loses.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_io.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_io/)

**Used in:** [Geometry from disk](../geometry_from_disk.md), [Meshes and 3D geometry](../mesh_examples.md), [Solids that cannot fail: Manifold in Field](../manifold.md)

## mesh_measure.kt { #mesh-measure-kt }

Asking a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) questions: how big is it, where is its middle, how curved is it — and, through
[`MeshBvh`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt-meshbvh), what does this ray hit, what is the nearest point on the surface, and is this point
inside.

The measurements (`TriMesh.surfaceArea`, `TriMesh.signedVolume`, `TriMesh.centroid`) are exact for
the polyhedron, computed in double precision, and cheap. `TriMesh.signedVolume` is the one to keep
in mind: it is the divergence-theorem tetrahedron sum, so it is exact for any closed mesh, it is
**positive for outward winding and negative for inward**, and comparing it against an analytic
answer (`4/3 π` for a marched unit sphere) is the single most informative test a geometry pipeline
can have.

The curvatures are the standard discrete operators — angle deficit for Gaussian, the
cotangent-Laplacian's magnitude for mean, both divided by the mixed Voronoi area. They satisfy
Gauss-Bonnet (`Σ K_v A_v = 2π χ`) to float precision on a closed mesh, which is how they are tested.

[`MeshBvh`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt-meshbvh) exists because the useful queries are all `O(n)` without it and `O(log n)` with it. It is
a plain median-split bounding-volume hierarchy over triangles, built once, then:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val bvh = mesh.bvh()
bvh.raycast(vec(0, 0, -5), vec(0, 0, 1))?.let { println("hit at ${it.point}") }
bvh.closestPoint(vec(2, 0, 0))                 // nearest surface point + distance
bvh.contains(vec(0, 0, 0))                     // inside test, by parity of crossings
bvh.signedDistance(vec(0.5f, 0, 0))            // negative inside
```

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_measure.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_measure/)

**Used in:** [Meshes and 3D geometry](../mesh_examples.md), [Three.js scenes with `three { … }`](../three_output.md)

## mesh_process.kt { #mesh-process-kt }

Changing a mesh's *sampling* without changing the shape it stands for: normals, subdivision,
smoothing and decimation.

These are the four operations that make the difference between a mesh you generated and a mesh you
can use. In rough order of how often you will reach for them:

 - `TriMesh.withVertexNormals` / `TriMesh.flatShaded` / `TriMesh.shadedNormals` — shading.
   `TriMesh.shadedNormals` splits a vertex only where the faces meeting there genuinely
   disagree, so a cylinder comes out smooth around its side and hard at its rim, from one call.
 - `TriMesh.loopSubdivide` — four triangles for one, converging on the Loop limit surface. Refines
   *and* smooths, and preserves the Euler characteristic exactly.
 - `TriMesh.laplacianSmooth` / `TriMesh.taubinSmooth` — noise removal. Laplacian shrinks the shape
   (that is what a diffusion does); Taubin's λ/μ pair alternates a shrink with an expand and so
   does not, which is why it is the one to default to. Both offer cotangent weights, which are
   scale- and shape-independent where the uniform ones are not.
 - `TriMesh.decimate` — quadric error metric edge collapse down to a triangle budget. The dual of
   subdivision, and the one that has to work hardest: it maintains per-vertex quadrics, a
   cost-ordered queue with lazy invalidation, the link condition (so a collapse cannot make the
   mesh non-manifold) and a normal-flip veto (so it cannot turn the mesh inside out locally).

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val fine = icosphereMesh(4)                       // 5120 triangles
val coarse = fine.decimate(400)                   // 400, and still a sphere
val smooth = coarse.taubinSmooth(iterations = 20) // volume preserved to within ~1%
```

Catmull-Clark is absent: it is a quad scheme, [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) is triangles-only, and
running it on a triangulated quad mesh gives a different (worse) surface than running it on the
quads. Loop is the triangle scheme, and it is the one here.

## mesh_repair.kt { #mesh-repair-kt }

Why a mesh is not a solid, and what can be done about it — the paved road between "I loaded a file"
and `toSolid()`.

`TriMesh.diagnose` answers *why*, in terms a person can act on: which loops are open and how big,
which edges have the wrong number of faces, which faces are duplicated, whether the winding is
consistent and whether it points out. `TriMesh.repairToSolid` then attempts the fixes in a
defensible order and hands back a [`MeshRepairResult`](graphics.md#mesh-repair-kt-meshrepairresult) that says **what it did and what it could
not do** — a repair that silently drops half your model is worse than one that refuses, so nothing
here returns a bare mesh.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val mesh = meshFromAnyFile("scan.glb")
println(mesh.diagnose().report())     // why it is not a solid, worst first
val fixed = mesh.repairToSolid()
println(fixed.report())               // what was done, and what was not
if (fixed.isSolid) display(fixed.mesh.toSolid() - drill)
```

### What actually blocks `toSolid`

Every severity below was established by feeding Manifold a mesh damaged in exactly one named way
(see `MeshDamage` in the tests) and asking whether it accepted the result. Three of the answers
change how a diagnosis should be read:

 - **A mesh with several disjoint components is fine.** Manifold accepts it and reports the sum of
   the volumes. "Split into parts" is not a defect; it is `MeshDefectKind.MULTIPLE_COMPONENTS`, and
   it is informational.
 - **Zero-area triangles are fine.** Manifold accepts them and the volume is unchanged.
 - **An inside-out mesh is fine, and that is the dangerous one.** Manifold accepts a consistently
   but inwardly wound closed surface and reports a **negative volume** — so the boolean you do next
   silently computes the wrong thing rather than throwing. That is
   `MeshDefectKind.INVERTED_ORIENTATION`, and it is the reason this file reports severity
   `MeshDefectSeverity.SUSPICIOUS` at all instead of just a pass/fail.

What Manifold genuinely rejects is a short list: a non-finite position, an edge with other than two
incident faces (which a duplicated face also produces, on all three of its edges), an open boundary,
and inconsistent winding.

### Which repair handles which defect

`TriMesh.repairToSolid` runs `TriMesh.repaired` first —
`weld → removeDegenerateTriangles → removeUnusedVertices → fixWinding` — which handles an
unwelded seam (welding is what turns an STL's pile of triangles into a surface) and inconsistent
winding. Of the twelve damaged meshes in `MeshRepairTest`'s table that Manifold rejects, that
alone fixes six.

Two families of damage need the repairs in this file:

 1. **Open boundaries** — `fillHoles`.
 2. **Non-manifold edges** — `removeDuplicateFaces` for a duplicated face,
    `removeNonManifoldFins` for a dangling fin.

## mesh_sdf.kt { #mesh-sdf-kt }

Modelling with functions: a [`ScalarField3D`](graphics.md#mesh-sdf-kt-scalarfield3d) is `(Vec3) -> Float`, the signed-distance primitives
and combinators that let you write a shape as an expression, and `marchingCubes`, which turns any
such expression into a watertight [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh).

This is the 3D counterpart of `contours.kt`. There, a [`ScalarField2D`](graphics.md#contours-kt-scalarfield2d) is marched by
`generateIsoContours` into `FLine` polylines; here a [`ScalarField3D`](graphics.md#mesh-sdf-kt-scalarfield3d) is marched into triangles.
The two files are parallel, and reading the 2D one first is the fastest way to
understand this one.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val body = sdfSmoothUnion(
    sdfSphere(0.8),
    sdfBox(vec(1.4, 0.25, 0.25)),
    k = 0.25,
)
val drilled = sdfSubtract(body, sdfCylinder(0.22, 3.0))
val mesh = marchingCubes(drilled, boundsOf(vec(-1.6, -1.6, -1.6), vec(1.6, 1.6, 1.6)), resolution = 96)
println("${mesh.triangleCount} tris, watertight ${mesh.isWatertight()}")
```

### What `marchingCubes` here actually does

It is a **topologically consistent** marching cubes, not the 1987 lookup table:

 - The field is sampled once per grid corner, so the cost is `(n+1)^3` evaluations however many
   triangles come out.
 - Every crossing sits on a grid *edge*, and edges are keyed globally, so a vertex is created once
   and **shared** by all the cubes that touch it. That is what makes the output watertight
   (`χ = 2` for a marched sphere) rather than a soup of unwelded triangles needing `TriMesh.weld`.
 - Instead of a 256-entry triangle table, each cube's crossings are joined into closed loops on the
   cube's own boundary and each loop is triangulated. On a face where four edges cross — the
   ambiguous case the classic table resolves arbitrarily — the pairing is chosen by the
   **asymptotic decider** (the sign of the bilinear saddle value). Because that decision is a pure
   function of the face's four corner values, the two cubes sharing the face always agree, which is
   exactly the property the classic table lacks and the reason plain marching cubes leaks.
 - Winding comes from the field itself: each triangle is oriented against the gradient of the
   trilinear interpolant, so normals point toward increasing field value — outward, for the
   signed-distance convention where outside is positive.

Known limits, stated rather than hidden: a cube containing two separate sheets of surface can be
oriented from one gradient and get the other sheet backwards, so a field with structure much finer
than the grid wants more resolution; and the loop triangulation reproduces the *sign pattern*
faithfully but is not guaranteed to reproduce the trilinear interpolant's exact topology in the
rarest configurations.

### A note on mutation

`Vec3` is mutable and the march reuses one sample vector for speed. A [`ScalarField3D`](graphics.md#mesh-sdf-kt-scalarfield3d) must
therefore **read** the vector it is handed and not write to it. Every combinator below copies
before transforming, so composing them is safe; a hand-written field that does `p.mul(2f)` will
corrupt the march.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_sdf.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_sdf/)

## mesh_topology.kt { #mesh-topology-kt }

What a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) *is*, as opposed to where it is: adjacency, boundaries, components,
manifoldness, orientation, and the Euler characteristic those add up to — plus the repairs
(`TriMesh.weld`, `TriMesh.fixWinding`, `TriMesh.removeDegenerateTriangles`) that turn a mesh
which fails those checks into one that passes.

[`MeshTopology`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt-meshtopology) is a **derived, cached** view: building one costs one pass over the triangles, and
everything after that is a lookup. Build it once and ask it many questions; the convenience
properties on [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) (`TriMesh.isWatertight` and friends) build a throwaway one each time,
which is fine interactively and wasteful in a loop.

The invariant the tests lean on: for a closed orientable surface, `V - E + F = 2 - 2g`. So a cube,
a sphere and an icosphere all report `MeshTopology.eulerCharacteristic` `2` and
`MeshTopology.genus` `0`, a torus reports `0` and `1`, and a two-holed shape reports `-2` and `2`.
A duplicated seam, a missing cap and an unwelded march all change that number, so it is the
cheapest single check on a generator.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val t = torusMesh(48, 24)
val topo = t.topology()
println("${topo.eulerCharacteristic} χ, genus ${topo.genus}, watertight ${topo.isWatertight}")
// 0 χ, genus 1, watertight true
```

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_topology.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_topology/)

**Used in:** [Meshes and 3D geometry](../mesh_examples.md), [Geometry from disk](../geometry_from_disk.md), [Solids that cannot fail: Manifold in Field](../manifold.md)

## pointing_mesh.kt { #pointing-mesh-kt }

Turning a place a person is looking at back into a place in the world.

This file does one step of that: **pixel → ray**, the unprojection that gets you from a mouse
position, a controller pose or a headset's aim to a line in the scene. [`PickScene`](graphics.md#pointing-pick-kt-pickscene) is the next
step, ray → named part, and [`Pointer`](graphics.md#pointing-pointer-kt-pointer) the step before, person → pixel-or-pose. Once you have the
ray, `MeshBvh.raycast`, `intersectRayTriangle` and `intersectRayPlane` answer what it hits.

### The two camera models

Field has two unrelated camera models, and confusing them is the main hazard here:

 - **[`MeshView`](graphics.md#mesh-field-kt-meshview)** — the orbital camera behind `TriMesh.renderPng`, Field's CPU rasterizer. Yaw,
   pitch, a distance *in multiples of the mesh's own bounding-sphere radius*, and a field of view.
   This is the one that makes pixels with no GPU, no window and no AWT, so it is the one a headless
   test or a docs capture can prove things with. `MeshView.rayCamera` inverts it, and does so by
   calling straight into `VisionGeometryPreview.ViewFrame` — *the same object the rasterizer
   projects with*, so the unprojection is the renderer's inverse by construction rather than by
   transcription.
 - **`afield.graphics.vulkan.util.Camera`** — the live Vulkan scene's camera: a `lookAt` model-view and a
   `afield.graphics.vulkan.util.SuperProjection`, which can be a perspective frustum, an off-centre one, an
   orthographic prism, or a Lie-group interpolation *between* perspective and ortho. There is no
   closed-form frustum to re-derive for that last case, so `rayCameraFor` handles all of them the
   same way: it inverts the clip matrix numerically, in double precision.

### Conventions

 - **Pixel coordinates run from the top-left of the frame, y downward**, which is what GLFW's
   cursor reports (`Window.cursor` is `glfwGetCursorPos`) and what an image's rows are indexed by.
   Pixel *centres* are at half-integers: pixel `(0, 0)` covers `[0,1) x [0,1)` and its centre is
   `(0.5, 0.5)`. All the `rayThroughPixel` overloads take the pixel *index* and aim at its centre.
 - **Field's clip space is Vulkan's depth range, `z` in `0..1`**, and `y` is *up* in NDC despite
   Vulkan's default being down — `afield.graphics.vulkan.Renderer` flips it with a negative-height viewport
   (`setViewportAndScissor` sets `y = rect.y + rect.h` and `height = -rect.h`), precisely so that
   the familiar GL-style projection matrices keep working. So NDC `y = +1` is the **top** row.
 - **A ray's direction is unit length**, so [`RayCamera`](graphics.md#pointing-kt-raycamera) hit distances are in world units and
   comparable between pointers.

### Typical use

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val mesh = icosphere(2)
val view = MeshView(yawDegrees = 30.0, pitchDegrees = 20.0)
val camera = view.rayCamera(mesh)
val hit = mesh.bvh().raycast(camera.rayThroughPixel(360, 270))
println(hit)                                  // the triangle under the middle of the picture
```

## FLineExact.kt { #flineexact-kt }

Curve-preserving boolean operations and cubic offsets for [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline), in the manner of Paper.js.

Booleans: every segment of both operands is cut at its exact crossings with every other segment
(Bézier–Bézier by bounding-box subdivision refined by Newton, plus endpoint-on-curve projection
for coincident edges and T-junctions). Each resulting piece is a sub-curve of an original
segment, so cubics stay cubics and straight segments stay `FLine.LineTo`. A piece is kept when
the operation's answer differs a hair to its left and to its right (winding numbers of both
operands, non-zero rule), oriented with the result on its left, and the kept pieces are chained
into closed contours. The result is checked against the java.awt.geom.Area answer by area; on
any failure the Area answer is returned instead (`FLineBooleanResult.exact` says which).

Offsets: each cubic is approximated by a cubic whose end tangents are the original's and whose
handle lengths are fitted to the true offset at the midpoint (Tiller–Hanson curvature scaling
where that fit is ill-conditioned), subdivided until the sampled error is within tolerance.
Corners get round, miter or bevel joins; closed results are resolved through the boolean engine
with a positive-winding rule, which removes the swallowtails at concave corners.

All arithmetic is in doubles over the xy plane; z is dropped.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/path/FLineExact.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/path/FLineExact/)

Planar curvature is signed (positive turns left); spatial curvature is unsigned. Costs a joint of 3 × parameters × dimensions values, so keep parameters to a few hundred. `step` defaults to a thousandth of the parameter span (at least 0.001); much smaller and the sampler can no longer resolve the difference between neighbouring velocities, understating the uncertainty. The same floor applies to a curve pinned so tightly that its velocity variance nears the `GpNumerics` tolerances; if `GpCurvature.std` changes with `step`, it is at that floor. |

## FLineGeometry.kt { #flinegeometry-kt }

Comprehensive computational geometry utilities for FLine operations implemented as extension functions.
Provides transformations, projections, intersections, decompositions, curvature analyses,
tangents, osculating planes, offsets, and a rich set of 2D and 3D geometric algorithms.

Functions that return new FLine instances use a "by" prefix to indicate non-mutating operations:
- `byWaving()` instead of `wave()`
- `byOffsetting()` instead of `offset()`

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/path/FLineGeometry.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/path/FLineGeometry/)

**Used in:** [FLine examples (Field graphics)](../fline_examples.md), [Functions to FLine examples (Field graphics)](../functions_examples.md), [Polytopes: topology first, coordinates later](../polytope_examples.md)

A line with no nodes has an empty `Rect(0, 0, 0, 0)`. |

Each subpath is closed back to its start if it is not already, and subpaths add: a counter wound the other way subtracts. Positive when the contours run counter-clockwise with y pointing **up** — which is clockwise on screen, where y points down. Paper.js `path.area`. |

## contours.kt { #contours-kt }

Marching-squares iso-contours for 2D scalar fields, plus the scalar field most callers want to
contour.

A field is just a [`ScalarField2D`](graphics.md#contours-kt-scalarfield2d), `(Double, Double) -> Double`. `pointEdgeScalarField2D` builds
one from points and edges — or from a 2D `FLine` — as the union of weighted discs and capsules,
signed so that `iso = 0.0` is the tube boundary; it re-reads the supplied point list on every
sample, so mutating those `Vec2`s moves the field live. `generateIsoContours` samples a field on
an `nx` by `ny` grid and returns stitched polylines, `generateIsoContoursWithStep` takes a target
cell size instead, and the `FLine` overloads choose the sampling window from the line's 2D bounds
grown by the tube radius.

`smoothIsoContours` and `generateSmoothIsoContours` fit cubic splines through the polylines,
treating a contour that ends on the sampling bounds as open and the rest as closed loops.

### Varying the radius along the line — weights

A tube of one radius is `pointRadius`/`edgeRadius`. To make it *taper*, weight the primitives:
every function that builds a point/edge field takes a **weight callback** rather than a list of
weights. On an explicit graph that is [`PointEdgeWeight`](graphics.md#contours-kt-pointedgeweight), `(index, point) -> Double`, indexed the
same way as the `points` you passed in. On an `FLine` it is [`FLinePointWeight`](graphics.md#contours-kt-flinepointweight),
`(nodeIndex, point) -> Double`, where `nodeIndex` is the *fractional* drawing-instruction index of
the flattened point — integral at a `moveTo`/`lineTo`, and interpolated across a `cubicTo`, which
is the same quantity `FLine.uniform_linearize` hands its callback and `linesOut` uses to look up
per-node colour. `FLine.isoWeights` is the stock implementation: it reads a per-node property and
interpolates between the nodes that set it.

It is a callback rather than a list of weights because on the `FLine` overloads there is no count
a caller could size a list against: the points and edges belong to `pointEdgeGraph2D`'s internal
flattening, and its edge count depends on the line's geometry as well as its instructions.

An edge's weight is always the **minimum** of its two endpoints'. A capsule has one radius for its
whole length and so cannot taper: the taper comes from the union of densely sampled discs, and the
edges only bridge the gaps between them. Taking the *maximum* would let a capsule bulge past the
disc envelope exactly where the weight changes fastest; the minimum fills the gap without ever
fattening it.

### The sign convention

A grid corner is *inside* iff its sample is **strictly below** `iso`; a sample exactly *at* `iso`
counts as outside. The test is two-valued rather than three-way, because under a three-way test —
`below` at one end of an edge, `above` at the other, so "equal" is neither — a sample sitting
exactly on `iso` suppresses the crossing on every edge out of its corner, and the contour
vanishes or shatters into arcs. Samples land exactly on `iso` for ordinary input: any grid that
samples a linear field at its own zero level puts a whole column there, and a unit circle
contoured at `iso = 0` passes through a grid corner at plenty of resolutions, `nx = ny = 16` over
`[-2, 2]` among them.

A crossing that lands on a corner is pushed off it by `ISO_CROSSING_EPSILON`, which moves it by
at most a thousandth of the cell edge it lies on — an analytic bound, since it is a `coerceIn` on
the interpolation parameter. `marchingCubes` in `mesh_sdf.kt` is the 3D marcher and uses the same
convention for the same reason.

### The saddle cell

A cell with four crossings is resolved by the *asymptotic decider*: the sign of the cell's
bilinear saddle value decides which diagonal pair of corners the centre of the cell belongs to.
It is a pure function of the cell's own four corner values, so two cells sharing an edge cannot
disagree about the crossing on it, which is what the stitcher needs. The ambiguity itself does
not go away: when the saddle value is exactly `iso` the two pairings are equally correct and the
decider has nothing to go on. `SADDLE_TIE_RELATIVE_EPSILON` settles that case in the code rather
than leaving it to the direction a multiplication rounded — which matters because every bilinear
field lands there exactly.

The segment stitcher is O(m^2) in the number of segments, so very high grid resolutions get
expensive.

## bspot.kt { #bspot-kt }

One-to-one matching between two equally sized 2D point clouds, at a million points a side, using
BSP-OT: every source point gets exactly one target and every target is used exactly once, with the
total squared travel distance kept small.

The exact answer to that problem is an assignment problem, and the Hungarian method that
`flowmatching.kt` uses for its minibatches is `O(n³)` time over an `n × n` cost matrix. At a
thousand points that is fine. At a million the matrix alone is four terabytes. BSP-OT gives up
provable optimality to get to `O(n log n)`:

1. Choose a direction. Split *each* cloud at its own median along it, so both left halves hold
   the same number of points, and so do both right halves.
2. Recurse, left with left and right with right, with a new direction each time. A leaf of one
   point pairs its source with its target; a leaf of two picks the cheaper of the two pairings.
3. That is one candidate bijection. Make several and merge each new one into the best so far: the
   union of two permutations falls apart into disjoint alternating cycles, and on each cycle you
   keep whichever orientation is cheaper. Then try two-point swaps along the candidate's edges.

The direction in step 1 is what `BspOt2D.Splits` chooses. The default, as in the reference
implementation, fits a Gaussian to each of the two subsets and splits along an eigenvector of the
linear map that carries one Gaussian onto the other, picking one of the two at random per node.
When the subsets differ in shape that axis is the one along which they need to move, and it
about halves the excess cost of random directions at eight trees. Below 50 points it stops fitting and splits
perpendicular to the parent.

The counts are equal by construction, not because the two clouds occupy the same cells, so clouds
of very different density still match completely.

    val result = matchPoints(from, to)            // two List<Vec2> of the same size
    val destination = result.reorder(to)          // destination`i` is where from`i` goes
    val halfway = from.indices.map { from`it` + (destination`it` - from`it`) * 0.5f }

For raw `FloatArray`s, call `BspOt2D.match` directly. A previous permutation can be passed as
`initial` and is improved rather than replaced, which suits matching successive frames of a
simulation.

### Cost, measured

On an M1 Max with the default four workers and eight trees, a million points a side takes 3 to
4.5 s for two uniform clouds, and 5.7 s from a uniform square onto three discs (7.4 s with random
splits, which reach a 5% higher cost). Merging is sequential. Array storage is about `69 + 60 P`
bytes a point for `P` workers, roughly 309 MB at a million points and four workers. The SIMD
paths (projection, and cost evaluation through a gather) gave no measurable end-to-end gain over
`simd = false` when this was first measured; partitioning, cycle walking and the swaps are
scalar.

### What it does not give you

- **No optimality guarantee, and further from optimal than the paper.** From a uniform square
  onto three discs, 1000 points, the total cost is 5.5% above the exact Hungarian answer with 8
  trees and 2.9% with 32. Two independent uniform clouds are the hard case: every node's two
  subsets have nearly the same Gaussian, so the transport map is close to the identity and its
  eigenvectors are noise. At 400 points that lands 26% above exact with 64 trees, where random
  splits reach 16%. Leaving those clouds unmatched is 120 times worse. The paper reports
  typically under 1% with 64 candidates; it ranks all candidates before merging, which this
  version, merging as it goes in bounded memory, does not. The bijection is good enough for a
  morph to read as a morph; it is not a solver for the exact assignment.
- **2D only, equal sizes only, uniform weights only.** No partial or unbalanced transport.
- **Deterministic for a given seed and options, across worker counts.** Not promised bit-identical
  across JDKs or CPUs.

Algorithm from Baptiste Genest, Nicolas Bonneel, Vincent Nivoliers and David Coeurjolly,
"BSP-OT: Sparse transport plans between discrete measures in loglinear time", ACM Transactions on
Graphics (SIGGRAPH Asia 2025), https://perso.liris.cnrs.fr/david.coeurjolly/publication/bspot-25/.
The Gaussian split follows `gaussianPartialBSPOT` and the merge `MergePlansNoPar` and
`BijectiveMatching::swapIfUpgrade` in their MIT-licensed
reference implementation, https://github.com/baptiste-genest/BSP-OT, Copyright (c) 2025 the same
authors.

## spatial_field.kt { #spatial-field-kt }

The bridges out of Field's plane-geometry results and into the things Field already draws.

Every partitioner in `graph_connectivity.kt`, `dirichlet.kt`, `contours.kt` and `clustering.kt`
answers with *structure* — cell vertex rings, circular arcs, triangle index triples, cluster
labels — and none of them answers with geometry. This file is the missing hop: one `toFLines` per
result type, so a Voronoi diagram, an Apollonius cell, a Delaunay triangulation or a k-medoids
partition lands in the same drawing, animation and export machinery as anything drawn by hand.
It is the plane counterpart of `mesh_field.kt`, which does the same job for `TriMesh`.

Two layers:

 1. **Structure → [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline).** `PointGraph.toFLine`, `delaunayTrianglesToFLine`,
    `VoronoiDiagram.toFLines`, `CircularDirichlet.Diagram.toFLines`,
    `CircularDirichlet.CellBoundary.toFLines`, `ClusterLayer.toFLines` and
    `pointCloudFLine`. Each returns styled, drawable lines and nothing else — no `Box`, no
    output, so they are usable from a test or a renderer as readily as from a box.
 2. **[`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) → a captioned figure.** `Box.showPlane` and `Box.showPlaneGrid` rasterise lines to
    inline SVG with `drawToSVG` and push a titled card — live and pannable for one figure, frozen
    for a grid of them — to a box output channel: the fastest way to see a whole pipeline at once,
    and the 2D twin of `Box.showMeshGrid`. `planeFigureHtml` is the markup on its own.

The figure helpers are AWT-free (Skia's SVG canvas, same as `Box.lines`), so they work headless,
including inside the docs build.

## stippling.kt { #stippling-kt }

Stippling: place exactly N points so that they follow an image's brightness *and* keep an even,
low-correlation ("blue-noise-ish") spacing from one another.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val dots = imgFromFile("face.png").stipple(5000)        // List<Vec2>, pixel coordinates
```

Sampling the brightness as a probability distribution gets the density right but clumps: two
independent samples are as likely to land on top of each other as anywhere else. This file instead
computes a **weighted centroidal Voronoi tessellation** (Secord's stippling) by Lloyd relaxation on
the CPU. Each iteration

1. rasterises the points into the pixel grid,
2. finds every pixel's nearest point with a separable exact Euclidean distance transform
   (a two-scan nearest-seed pass along each row, then Felzenszwalb–Huttenlocher's lower envelope of
   parabolas down each column), which yields the Voronoi cells as a label raster in `O(pixels)`
   regardless of the point count,
3. moves each point to the density-weighted centroid of its cell.

The rows and columns are split across a fork-join pool of their own, and nothing on the per-iteration
path allocates: the label rasters, the column scratch and the per-worker centroid accumulators are
all allocated once, in the constructor.

### Where the points go, and what relaxation does not change

The *number* of points in a region is decided by the starting sample. Relaxation evens out the
spacing between neighbours and moves hardly any points from one region to another, so the point
density is whatever the start gave, `brightness^densityPower`. With the default of 1, points follow
brightness, and a larger power exaggerates contrast.

That makes the start matter. An independent weighted random sample has the right density on
average and random clumps everywhere, and relaxation keeps the clumps' counts: on a flat field the
count variance in 48-pixel windows is 0.60 of a random scatter's after relaxing, which reads as
blotches in a mid tone. So the start is stratified along a Hilbert curve instead. The curve visits
the image in a way that keeps nearby pixels nearby, it is cut into `count` stretches of equal
density, and each stretch gets one point. Every region the curve covers then starts with its exact
share, and the same measurement after relaxing is 0.028.

Theory predicts a different density: the *optimal* centroidal tessellation of a density `ρ` in 2-D
has point density `ρ^(1/2)`. Lloyd iteration from a weighted start does not travel there. On a
field half at brightness 1 and half at 0.5 the bright/dim count ratio stays at 2 through hundreds of
iterations, against an optimum of 1.41, until the iteration reaches a fixed point on the raster
where `Stippler.step` returns 0. `StipplingTest` pins both powers, the drift and the lumpiness.

### Memory

Besides five rasters of `supersample² * width * height` pixels, each worker keeps its own three
`DoubleArray(count)` centroid accumulators so that workers never contend. That is cheap at ten or a hundred thousand
points, and 384 MB at a million points on 16 workers — pass a smaller `threads` there.

## voronoi.kt { #voronoi-kt }

Practical 3D Voronoi and approximate 3D multiplicatively weighted Voronoi
("CircularDirichlet") for Kotlin + Field linalg.

- `voronoi3d` builds convex polyhedral cells by intersecting pairwise bisector half-spaces. Six
  clip-box planes are added to **every** cell, not only to the unbounded ones, so a cell always
  comes back as a bounded polyhedron; `VoronoiCell3.bounded` is how you tell whether the answer is
  the site's own cell or an artefact of the box. The box is the sites' bounding box grown on every
  side by `clipPadding * scale + 1`, where `scale` is the cloud's own diagonal (floored at 1).
- `CircularDirichlet3d.build` extracts approximate support patches on bisector spheres / planes by
  clipping a sampled surface mesh with the weighted score predicate.

The weighted contourer is renderer-oriented: it prefers stable, wound
boundary loops over exact symbolic patch topology.

### How the unweighted clipper assigns a corner to a face

**Combinatorially**: a corner records the planes that produced it, and a face's polygon is exactly
the corners recording that plane. Not by a distance test against a tolerance — a tolerance scaled
off the point cloud lets faces near a near-cospherical site cluster claim corners that are not on
them, and then the cells do not close, which is a T-junction and a hairline crack in any mesh
built from the faces. The `collectCorners` KDoc in [`Voronoi3d`](graphics.md#voronoi-kt-voronoi3d) has the detail.

Closure is not total, because the clipper works in `Float`: **4 of 465 bounded cells** and **12 of
447 clipped cells** fail the strict check that every edge is walked by exactly two faces in
opposite directions. `VoronoiFaceTopologyTest` pins both counts with `<=`, so they can improve but
cannot regress silently. Cell volumes tile the clip box to 1e-4 relative, and a cubic lattice of
sites gives exact unit cubes.

## Colormaps.kt { #colormaps-kt }

The colour vocabulary the visualization helpers share: [`Color4`](graphics.md#colormaps-kt-color4), a `[0,1]`-component colour value
with no dependencies, and [`Colormaps`](graphics.md#colormaps-kt-colormaps), eight named ramps that can be sampled at any parameter.

A ramp here is a short table of evenly-spaced control points rather than a 256-entry lookup table
(nine colours for each of the matplotlib maps, seventeen for turbo, three for the house
cyan→orange), and `Colormaps.sampleStops` interpolates linearly between them. A caller that
colours one pixel at a time builds its own table from that: `showHeatmap` quantises the ramp into
1024 entries once per image rather than interpolating per pixel.

Names are matched after trimming and lowercasing, `gray`, `greys` and `cyan-orange` are aliases,
and an unknown name raises with `Colormaps.names` in the message rather than falling back to a
default. RectSL's `colormap` and `cmap` words, `showHeatmap` and the imaging visualizers all take
that same vocabulary, so a ramp named in one place is the same ramp in another.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/color/Colormaps.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/color/Colormaps/)

**Used in:** [Imaging and computer vision](../imaging_examples.md)
