### Colormaps { #colormaps-kt-colormaps }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">Colormaps</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/color/Colormaps/#L89)

Perceptually-uniform colormaps as named colour ramps — matplotlib's viridis / magma / plasma / inferno, Google's turbo, Kenneth Moreland's coolwarm diverging map, and a plain grayscale. Each map is a table of evenly-spaced RGB control points taken from the published data (the viridisLite 9-class swatches for the matplotlib family, the turbo_srgb_floats LUT sampled every 16th entry, Moreland's cool→warm table); `sampleStops` interpolates linearly between them. This is reusable domain code — the single source of truth for the `showHeatmap` visualizer and RectSL's `colormap`/`cmap`, `bars`, `heat`, and `scatter` words, and directly callable from Kotlin.

## colors.kt { #colors-kt }

Colour constructors for the stdlib. Everything here returns a `Vec4` of sRGB-encoded components
clamped to `[0,1]` with alpha last, so the results drop straight into FLine colours and uniforms.

`rgb` / `rgba` accept either 0..1 or 0..255 components — the scale is inferred per call from
whether any component exceeds 1 — and `rgb255` forces the 0..255 reading. `hsl` is HSL with the
usual cube geometry, but the result is encoded through the sRGB transfer function on the way out,
so it is *not* interchangeable with CSS `hsl()` — see `hsl` for what that costs. `okhsl` and
`okhsv` are the Oklab-based equivalents; of the two only `okhsl` holds perceived lightness steady
across hue, because `okhsv` scales `v` against the per-hue gamut cusp exactly as HSV always has.
Hue may be given as a fraction of a turn or in degrees (magnitude above 1 is divided
by 360) and is wrapped either way.

For sets: `hueSetHsl`, `hueSetOkhsl` and `hueSetOkhsv` (aliased `hslSet`, `okhslSet`, `okhsvSet`)
space equally-separated hues around the wheel at a fixed saturation and lightness.
`paletteForBackground` starts from the same okhsl ring but then walks each entry's lightness up
or down until it clears a minimum WCAG contrast ratio against the supplied background, returning
the highest-contrast candidate it found when it cannot reach the target.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/color/colors.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/color/colors/)

**Used in:** [Colors to FLine examples](../colors_examples.md)

## pointing.kt { #pointing-kt }

Turning a place a person is looking at back into a place in the world.

This file does one step of that: **pixel → ray**, the unprojection that gets you from a mouse
position, a controller pose or a headset's aim to a line in the scene. [`PickScene`](graphics.md#pointing-pick-kt-pickscene) is the next
step, ray → named part, and [`Pointer`](graphics.md#pointing-pointer-kt-pointer) the step before, person → pixel-or-pose. Once you have the
ray, `MeshBvh.raycast`, `intersectRayTriangle` and `intersectRayPlane` answer what it hits.

### The two camera models

Field has two unrelated camera models, and confusing them is the main hazard here:

 - **[`MeshView`](graphics.md#mesh-field-kt-meshview)** — the orbital camera behind `TriMesh.renderPng`, Field's CPU rasterizer. Yaw,
   pitch, a distance *in multiples of the mesh's own bounding-sphere radius*, and a field of view.
   This is the one that makes pixels with no GPU, no window and no AWT, so it is the one a headless
   test or a docs capture can prove things with. `MeshView.rayCamera` inverts it, and does so by
   calling straight into `VisionGeometryPreview.ViewFrame` — *the same object the rasterizer
   projects with*, so the unprojection is the renderer's inverse by construction rather than by
   transcription.
 - **`afield.graphics.vulkan.util.Camera`** — the live Vulkan scene's camera: a `lookAt` model-view and a
   `afield.graphics.vulkan.util.SuperProjection`, which can be a perspective frustum, an off-centre one, an
   orthographic prism, or a Lie-group interpolation *between* perspective and ortho. There is no
   closed-form frustum to re-derive for that last case, so `rayCameraFor` handles all of them the
   same way: it inverts the clip matrix numerically, in double precision.

### Conventions

 - **Pixel coordinates run from the top-left of the frame, y downward**, which is what GLFW's
   cursor reports (`Window.cursor` is `glfwGetCursorPos`) and what an image's rows are indexed by.
   Pixel *centres* are at half-integers: pixel `(0, 0)` covers `[0,1) x [0,1)` and its centre is
   `(0.5, 0.5)`. All the `rayThroughPixel` overloads take the pixel *index* and aim at its centre.
 - **Field's clip space is Vulkan's depth range, `z` in `0..1`**, and `y` is *up* in NDC despite
   Vulkan's default being down — `afield.graphics.vulkan.Renderer` flips it with a negative-height viewport
   (`setViewportAndScissor` sets `y = rect.y + rect.h` and `height = -rect.h`), precisely so that
   the familiar GL-style projection matrices keep working. So NDC `y = +1` is the **top** row.
 - **A ray's direction is unit length**, so [`RayCamera`](graphics.md#pointing-kt-raycamera) hit distances are in world units and
   comparable between pointers.

### Typical use

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val mesh = icosphere(2)
val view = MeshView(yawDegrees = 30.0, pitchDegrees = 20.0)
val camera = view.rayCamera(mesh)
val hit = mesh.bvh().raycast(camera.rayThroughPixel(360, 270))
println(hit)                                  // the triangle under the middle of the picture
```

## pointing_pick.kt { #pointing-pick-kt }

A scene you can point at, and a hit record that names the **part** you touched rather than the
triangle.

### Why a triangle index is not an answer

`MeshBvh.raycast` returns a [`RayHit`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt-rayhit), and `RayHit.triangle` is an index into an [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh)'s
`indices` array. That is the right thing for a physics query and the wrong thing for a person: a
human pointing at a house wants to hear *"the east wall"*, not *"triangle 4471"*, and a triangle
index changes every time the geometry is rebuilt, so it cannot be written down, logged, compared
between two runs or used as a selection.

So a pickable carries [`PickParts`](graphics.md#pointing-pick-kt-pickparts) — a per-triangle part id with names — and a [`PickHit`](graphics.md#pointing-pick-kt-pickhit) reports
the part. Three things then become possible that were not: naming the thing you touched, keeping
a selection across a re-render, and asking whether two pointers found *the same* part.

### Where a part id comes from

In descending order of how much it is worth trusting:

 1. **The geometry already knows.** `PickParts.fromTriangulated` reads
    `TriangulatedGeometry.sourceFace` — the polytope layer has recorded, for every triangle it
    emits, the polygonal face it was cut from — well covered by the polytope tests and, until now,
    read by nothing in `jvmMain` outside `polytope` itself. This is the only
    source here where the id means something *outside* the mesh: it is an
    [`afield.geometry.polytope.ElementId`](polytopes.md#topology-kt-elementid) in the polytope's own topology, so it survives
    re-triangulation with a different triangulator and can be handed back to the polytope API.
 2. **The author said so.** `PickParts.of` takes the array, for a builder that knows which
    triangles it just appended — see `TriMeshBuilder.groups`, which records it for you.
 3. **The topology can guess.** `PickParts.byComponent` splits on connected components. Cheap and
    cheap, and exactly as good as the mesh's connectivity: a house whose walls all share vertices
    is one component and therefore one part, which is a real limitation and not a bug here.

#### What happens when the geometry is rebuilt

[`PickParts`](graphics.md#pointing-pick-kt-pickparts) is **keyed by triangle index and valid only for the mesh it was built from.**
[`Pickable`](graphics.md#pointing-pick-kt-pickable) checks the triangle count on construction, which catches the gross case; it cannot
catch a mesh of the same size with different triangles, and does not pretend to. If you rebuild
geometry every frame, rebuild the [`PickParts`](graphics.md#pointing-pick-kt-pickparts) with it and carry the *part id* — never the triangle
— across the rebuild. That is the whole reason ids exist.

### Typical use

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val scene = pickScene {
    add("floor", plane(4.0), parts = PickParts.single(plane(4.0), "floor"))
    add("lamp", icosphere(2), at = Matrix4f().translation(0f, 1.5f, 0f))
}
val camera = MeshView().rayCamera(scene.mergedMesh())
val hit = scene.pick(camera.rayThroughPixel(360, 270))
println(hit?.describe())      // "lamp / lamp  tri 812  1.83 away  at (0.31, 1.72, 0.44)"
```

## pointing_pointer.kt { #pointing-pointer-kt }

A person pointing — mouse, XR controller or pinched hand — behind one interface, and the
hover / press / drag / release machine that turns a stream of samples into an interaction.

### A pointer is three things

A ray, a select value in `0..1`, and whether it exists at all ([`PointerState`](graphics.md#pointing-pointer-kt-pointerstate)). That is enough to
unify every pointing device Field can see:

 - **A mouse** has a ray only because a camera can be inverted (`mousePointer`), a select value
   that is `0` or `1`, and is always active while the window has a cursor.
 - **An XR controller** has a pose and a trigger, and reports `active` when the runtime is tracking
   it (`controllerPointer`).
 - **A pinched hand** has 26 joints and a geometric pinch strength, read off
   `afield.graphics.vulkan.targets.OpenXRHmdTarget`'s `handState`. Its select value is continuous and noisy,
   which is what the second half of this file is about (`pinchPointer`).

### Hysteresis, in two places

Feed raw nearest-hit results to a UI and it flickers. There are two flickers here and
[`PointerInteraction`](graphics.md#pointing-pointer-kt-pointerinteraction) treats them separately:

 1. **The part flickers** when the ray lands near an edge two parts share, or grazes a silhouette.
   A pixel's worth of hand tremor alternates the answer every frame, and a label that alternates
   every frame is unreadable. The fix is a **dwell** guarding every transition *away* from a held
   hover — see `PointerInteraction.switchSamples` and the rule stated on `resolveHover`. Acquiring
   a hover is never delayed, because a lag between pointing at something and it lighting up reads
   as the pointer being broken.
 2. **The click flickers** when a continuous select value sits on the threshold — which a
   geometric `pinchStrength` derived from a 40 mm range of finger separation does constantly. The
   fix is a **Schmitt trigger**: press at `PointerInteraction.pressThreshold`, release at the lower
   `PointerInteraction.releaseThreshold`. A value wobbling between them holds its state.

And once pressed, **the drag belongs to what it grabbed**: hover is frozen, and
`PointerInteraction.dragOffset` reports where the ray now crosses the plane through the original
contact point, so letting the pointer wander off the object does not drop the drag.

### Typical use

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val scene = pickScene { add("model", mesh, parts = builder.groups()) }
val pointer = mousePointer(camera = { view.rayCamera(mesh) }, cursor = { window.cursor },
                           selecting = { window.isMouseButtonPressed(GLFW_MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT) })
val interaction = PointerInteraction(scene)
forever {
    interaction.update(pointer.sample())
    if (interaction.justPressed) println("grabbed ${interaction.grabbed?.partName}")
}
```

### TriangleCluster { #clustergeometry-kt-trianglecluster }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">TriangleCluster</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">firstVertex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">firstIndex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">vertexCount</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">triangleCount</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">clusterId</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">geometryId</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/ClusterGeometry/#L25)

One Field cluster description, eight uint32 words / 32 bytes, usable by ordinary compute shaders. Positions are vec4 (xyz in world/object units); indices are uint32 LOCAL to this cluster's vertex slice. A cluster may change counts, positions and indices on every build. IDs stay yours. Invalid GPU records become degenerate geometry and set `ClusterGeometry.status` rather than passing unchecked addresses/counts to Vulkan. No host readback occurs during builds.

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">ClusterGeometryInput</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">positions</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">VulkanBuffer</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">indices</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">VulkanBuffer</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">clusters</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">VulkanBuffer</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/ClusterGeometry/#L38)

Borrowed producer buffers. Keep alive through build completion; synchronize any subsequent writes. `clusters` contains [`TriangleCluster`](graphics.md#clustergeometry-kt-trianglecluster) records. Buffer sizes, not arbitrary user-supplied addresses, determine bounds in the GPU validation/conversion pass.

### ClusterGeometry { #clustergeometry-kt-clustergeometry }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">ClusterGeometry</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">renderer</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Renderer</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">capacity</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">verticesPerCluster</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="mi">128</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">trianglesPerCluster</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="mi">128</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maxGeometryId</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AccelerationStructureAddress</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="nc">AutoCloseable</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/ClusterGeometry/#L46)

General NV Mega Geometry builder: Field compute -> validated clusters -> CLAS -> one cluster BLAS. It owns bounded build/storage/scratch resources, never producer buffers. Single graphics queue; call `build` explicitly after a producer changes geometry. Static geometry needs only one build. Recreate to increase capacity. A rebuild changes this BLAS's bounds: rebuild the containing TLAS. Cluster BLAS has an address but no VkAccelerationStructure handle; use it in [`RayTracingInstance`](graphics.md#accelerationstructure-kt-raytracinginstance).

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">ClusterGeometryDemo</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">renderer</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Renderer</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">columns</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="mi">32</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">rows</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="mi">24</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">width</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="mi">1920</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">height</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="mi">1080</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s">&quot;computed-clusters&quot;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">producerFactory</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">Parameters</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="o">-&gt;</span><span class="nc">ComputeModulePointer</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="p">{</span><span class="nc">ComputeModule</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="kc">it</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">pointer</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Target</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="nc">AutoCloseable</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/ClusterGeometryDemo/#L21)

Computed terrain, using exactly the public ClusterGeometry input contract. The producer shader owns all vertices, indices and descriptions, and is replaceable through ordinary live reload. Each patch has 8x8 cells; `topology` switches diagonals without changing allocations.

| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">onCreated</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/ModuleRebuild/#L60) | Called when a module has just made its uniform structures, before anything has written them. A uniform buffer starts as whatever memory it was given, so a member that must read as zero until set — a `stack.auto` numbers block's `foo_live` — is written here. |

## StandardDrawing.kt { #standarddrawing-kt }

The small vocabulary of `FLine` construction and styling that sketches and examples reach for
first.

`fline` is the builder; the `rangeTo` operator makes a one-segment line out of two vectors
(`a..b`, composable with `+=`), and the styling overloads of `moveTo` / `lineTo` / `cubicTo`
position a node and style it in the same call. Appearance is carried by delegated properties on
`FLine` and `FLine.Node` — `color`, `thickness`, `thicken`, `filled`, `stroked`, `pointed`,
`pointSize` — which the renderers read back; `onClick` and `hoverColor` only do anything in the
interactive outputs.

The rest are shape helpers: `rect` and `Rect.toFLine`, `arrow` (a real filled arrowhead rather
than a point sprite), `seg`, and `fitInto`, which scales and centres a list of lines into a
`Rect` using their 2D bounds only.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/render/StandardDrawing.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/StandardDrawing/)

**Used in:** [FLine examples (Field graphics)](../fline_examples.md), [Three.js scenes with `three { … }`](../three_output.md), [Points into structure — Voronoi, Apollonius, contours and clusters](../spatial_geometry_examples.md)

### Top-level values { #standarddrawing-kt-values }

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">color</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vector4f</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/StandardDrawing/#L124) | The line's colour as RGBA in `0..1` (sRGB, alpha included) — one colour for the stroke, the fill and the node dots alike. Opaque white when never set. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">Node</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">color</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vector4f</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/StandardDrawing/#L135) | Per-node colour override in `0..1`, which is how one FLine carries a gradient: the GPU point/triangle writers in `afield.graphics.render.StandardDrawing` use a node's own colour where it has one and the whole line's `color` where it does not. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">thickness</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="o">?</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/StandardDrawing/#L141) | Stroke width, in the same units as the line's own points (pixels, for the 2D outputs). `null` — the default — means "unset", which every renderer reads as 1.0 rather than as "invisible". |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">thicken</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Stroke</span><span class="o">?</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/StandardDrawing/#L151) | An AWT `Stroke` that replaces "stroke at one width" with "convert this line into the outline of its own stroke" — dashes, tapers, calligraphic pens, anything `Stroke.createStrokedShape` can do. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">filled</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/StandardDrawing/#L157) | Whether closed subpaths are flooded with `color`. `false` by default, and independent of `stroked` — with both true the renderers fill and then draw the outline on top. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">stroked</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/StandardDrawing/#L164) | Whether the path is stroked at `thickness`. `true` by default; with this and `filled` both false the geometry still exists and still hit-tests, but nothing is drawn except the node dots that `pointed` asks for. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">pointed</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/StandardDrawing/#L171) | Draw a dot at every node of the line — every `moveTo`/`lineTo`/`cubicTo` endpoint, not the interior control points of a cubic and not `close`. Off by default. The fast way to see where a path's points actually landed, and how a particle set gets drawn at all. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">pointSize</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/StandardDrawing/#L180) | Size of the dots `pointed` draws, 1.0 by default, overridable node by node with `FLine.Node.pointSize`. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">Node</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">pointSize</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="o">?</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/StandardDrawing/#L187) | Per-node override of the line's `FLine.pointSize`, under the same `* 3` radius convention. `null` — the default, and unlike the line-level property this one is not written back on read — means "follow the line". |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">onClick</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">FLineIntersection</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">-</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/StandardDrawing/#L312) | Callback invoked when this FLine is clicked in an interactive output. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">label</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/StandardDrawing/#L321) | A human name for this line, reported back as `FLineIntersection.label` when it is clicked and used as the heading by `afield.ui.visualization.inspect`. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">hoverColor</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec4</span><span class="o">?</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/StandardDrawing/#L327) | Color to show when the pointer hovers over this FLine in an interactive SVG output. When null no hover color change is applied. |

### FLineHitKind { #standarddrawing-kt-flinehitkind }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">FLineHitKind</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/StandardDrawing/#L197)

What kind of thing on a figure a click landed on — the same three-way distinction the editable FLine widget already draws its hit targets with (`data-fline-hit-kind` in `sliders.js`), now reported to `FLine.onClick` as well.

Constants: `POINT`, `EDGE`, `FACE`, `UNKNOWN`.

### FLineFaceCoordinates { #standarddrawing-kt-flinefacecoordinates }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">FLineFaceCoordinates</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/StandardDrawing/#L215)

Which convention `FLineIntersection.u` and `v` follow for a `FLineHitKind.FACE` hit — because there is no one right answer for a face nobody chose, and a plausible wrong number is worse than a labelled one.

Constants: `NONE`, `BILINEAR`, `BOUNDING_BOX`.

class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">onElement</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec3</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/StandardDrawing/#L247)

Hit information passed to `FLine.onClick` from the interactive line renderers — what a click on a figure *returns*.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">closestVertexIndex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Index into the line's `nodes` of the node nearest the click, or `-1` when the client did not work one out. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">position</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec3</span></code> | Where the click landed, in the line's own coordinate space. The three.js output fills in all three components; the 2D SVG output leaves `z` at 0 — `onElement` is the one to read for a depth, because it interpolates `z` along the element that was hit. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">kind</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">FLineHitKind</span></code> | Which kind of element was hit. `FLineHitKind.UNKNOWN` when the output does not distinguish. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">lineIndex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Index of the clicked line within the lines passed to that one `lines(...)` call, or `-1` when unknown. The point of it: one shared `onClick` closure can serve a whole figure, instead of one closure per part. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">label</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | The clicked line's `FLine.label`, if it had one. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">nodeIndex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Index into the line's `nodes` of the node that *is* this element: the node itself for a `FLineHitKind.POINT`, the node that draws the segment for an `FLineHitKind.EDGE`, the `Close` for a `FLineHitKind.FACE`. `-1` when unknown. Unlike `closestVertexIndex` this is the element, not the nearest dot. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">subPathIndex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Which subpath (`moveTo`-delimited piece) of the line the element belongs to, or `-1`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">elementIndex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Ordinal of the element among its own kind within the line — edge 0, 1, 2…; face 0, 1… Or `-1`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">u</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Where on the element the click landed, `0..1`, or `NaN` when it does not apply. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">v</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | The second face coordinate for an `FLineHitKind.FACE`, `NaN` otherwise. See `faceCoordinates`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">faceCoordinates</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">FLineFaceCoordinates</span></code> | Which convention `u` and `v` follow for a face hit — bilinear on a four-corner face, its bounding box otherwise, or a refusal. Always `FLineFaceCoordinates.NONE` for a non-face hit. |

Raster surface contract. XYZ world position + Vulkan depth [0,1] (clear=1, not reversed); XYZ world shading normal; linear RGB albedo. Motion is currentUV-previousUV, Y down, unjittered. Point sampling only. Material identity, emission, eligibility and temporal validity are NOT alpha. The optional RTXDI bridge snapshots these inputs; material IDs are not encoded in alpha.

### OpaqueRayScene { #opaquerayscene-kt-opaquerayscene }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">OpaqueRayScene</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">renderer</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Renderer</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">HasAccelerationStructure</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">AutoCloseable</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/lighting/OpaqueRayScene/#L41)

Static BLAS per geometry identity; a new TLAS for each explicit instance edit. No refit is claimed. Commit on the render thread between frames. Builds submit on Field's graphics queue and wait for their fence; removed resources retire via Field's frames-in-flight queue. This intentionally conservative first slice makes edits safe, at the cost of a stall on instance/topology edits.

## megaTextures.kt { #megatextures-kt }

A directory of images as one texture, however many of them there are.

`Box.megaTextureHere` is the whole box-facing surface: point it at a folder and it scans the
folder, builds the atlas, and registers the GLSL your shaders interpolate with `{{ mega.all }}`.
The machinery behind it lives in `afield.graphics.texture.mega`, and the reason it is worth reaching
for rather than a pile of `LoadedTexture`s is that it is *GPU-driven*: the fragment shader
measures its own on-screen footprint and asks for the resolution it needs, so nothing here has to
be told where anything is or how big it looks.

`dev_docs/agents/transcripts/mega_texture_wall.yaml` is the worked example — five lines of Kotlin
and two shaders you can edit live.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/render/megaTextures.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/megaTextures/)

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">OpenDlssNrPass</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">renderer</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Renderer</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">width</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">height</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AutoCloseable</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/render/neural/OpenDlssNrPass/#L49)

Optional native Vulkan pass, recorded outside render passes on Field's graphics queue. Construct/evaluate/edit/close on the renderer thread. Recreate at a new resolution; close retires behind Field's completion fences. The output is linear RGBA16F, ready for normal Field grading. No CPU frame transfer or private per-frame submit occurs. Failure is explicit; callers can use availability() before creating the pass and present the source when unavailable.

### ShaderBindingKind { #shaderinterfacetransition-kt-shaderbindingkind }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">ShaderBindingKind</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">label</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/shader/ShaderInterfaceTransition/#L10)

The kinds of thing a shader's interface binds, as a full reload compares them. `label` is how a transition summary names one: "uniform block `Light` grew 16→32 bytes".

Constants: `UNIFORM_BLOCK`, `STORAGE_BUFFER`, `TEXTURE`, `IMAGE`, `ACCELERATION_STRUCTURE`, `PUSH_CONSTANT`.

### GpuShaderTraining { #gpushadertraining-kt-gpushadertraining }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">GpuShaderTraining</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">renderer</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Renderer</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">width</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">height</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">batchSize</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="mi">256</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">seed</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="mi">42</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="nc">AutoCloseable</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/shader/learning/GpuShaderTraining/#L36)

A small reusable learned RGB function, trained directly from Field images on the graphics queue. Architecture matches LearnedShader: 16 positional features -> 32 ReLU -> 32 ReLU -> RGB. Slang differentiates the network; cooperative-vector outer products accumulate its gradients. FP32 Adam master weights/moments, loss-scaled FP16 gradients and inference matrices. The source remains caller-owned. Train/evaluate/close only between or within render-thread work. No CPU image/weight readback is used in train/evaluate. This is not a general graph ML runtime.

## shaders.kt { #shaders-kt }

The bridge between a box's text and a live Vulkan pipeline: shader source lives in box
properties, and this file turns it into modules and keeps them hot-reloading.

The properties come first — `vertex`, `fragment`, `compute`, `task`/`mesh`, the ray-tracing
stages, and a `_s` variant of each for Slang — alongside `once.vertex { }`-style seeders. The
user-facing entry points are the macro placeholders `Box.moduleHere`, `Box.computeModuleHere`,
`Box.meshModuleHere`, `Box.rayTracingModuleHere` and `Box.shadertoyHere`; each one throws
`MacroNotExpandedException` if actually called, because `MacroRegistry` is expected to rewrite it
into the real `_moduleHere`-family call.

Before compilation every stage goes through `preprocess`, which resolves `{% include %}` template
tags against other boxes' shader properties (with cycle detection and `#line` fixups) and against
built-in includes such as the field probe, field stats and quantile warp. Registered include roots —
`registerShaderFilesystemIncludeRoot` for a directory, `registerLygiaIncludeRoot` /
`shaderCachedUrlIncludeRootResolver` for URL-fetched, disk-cached libraries — are **not** reachable
from here: they are resolved by shaderc during compilation, from a real `#include` only. It also expands
`{% copyPC %}` (copying a previous stage's push-constant block) and stackAuto template slots
compiled from StackSL via `stackAutoShaderSource`.

`reloadShader`, `reloadComputeShader`, `reloadMeshShader` and `reloadRayTracingShader` are the
reload path: compile, report errors back onto the box's source lines, introspect the result, and
rewrite the box's Kotlin preamble with generated binding structures before swapping the module.
`Box.attachShader` adopts an externally built module into that same path. `Box.fieldProbeHere`,
`Box.fieldStatsHere` and `Box.fieldProbeAutoControl` attach the GPU readback instrumentation.

Everything here needs a live `Box` — properties, error reporting, preamble edits and the
generation-guarded async reload all key off it.

### StackAutoReport { #shaders-kt-stackautoreport }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">StackAutoReport</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">compiled</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">problems</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">&gt;</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">emptyList</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">warnings</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">&gt;</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">emptyList</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">notes</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">&gt;</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">emptyList</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">errors</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">&gt;</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">emptyList</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ToHTML</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/shader/shaders/#L615)

What compiling one `stack.auto` slot had to say beyond "it compiled" — the warnings, and the stack arithmetic that says whether the program is shaped the way its author thinks.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | The slot this is about — the `foo` of `{{ stack.auto.foo }}`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">compiled</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | False when the program has an ERROR diagnostic, which is then in `errors`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">problems</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | Almost certainly bugs. A definition whose net stack effect is not "consume one, leave one". |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">warnings</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | The compiler's own non-ERROR diagnostics: warnings and notes from a compile that succeeded. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">notes</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | Worth seeing, not worth failing on — chiefly how much computed work nothing consumes. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">errors</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | Why it did not compile: the compiler's ERROR diagnostics, empty when `compiled`. Until 2026-09-29 a failed report carried none of them — `warnings` leaves errors out — so a slot study refusing a candidate said "does not compile into stack.auto.foo:" and then nothing. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">quiet</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/shader/shaders/#L635) | Nothing to say: it compiled, no warnings, every definition balanced, nothing pruned. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">lines</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/shader/shaders/#L638) | Every line, most serious first, for a log or a one-shot println. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">override</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">toHTML</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/shader/shaders/#L645) | The report as a small monospaced card: one coloured line per problem, warning and note, and a dim "clean" when there is nothing to say. This is what the `stack.auto` output channel shows. |

## typography.kt { #typography-kt }

Text as geometry: a string becomes contours, and from there everything Field already does to
geometry applies to letters.

A layout here is a value you can extrude, march, sample or animate, not a label painted into a
raster — which is what every other use of `java.awt.Font` in the tree does (`MeshGallery`,
`ImagingGallery`, `montage`'s 5x7 bitmap font). It needs no dependency beyond AWT:
`Font.createGlyphVector(...).getOutline()` hands back real quadratic/cubic glyph outlines, and it
works headless. `typography_field.kt` is the bridge to Field's own 2D and 3D outputs.

### The three values

 - [`Typeface`](graphics.md#typography-kt-typeface) — a font at a size, from a logical/system name (`typeface`) or a `.ttf`/`.otf` on
   disk (`typefaceFromFile`). Carries the vertical metrics (ascent, descent, leading) a layout
   needs.
 - [`Glyph`](graphics.md#typography-kt-glyph) — one glyph's outline, cached per typeface and glyph code, in its own frame with its
   origin on its own baseline. Both representations live side by side: `Glyph.contours` are
   flattened, nesting-classified, winding-normalised polygons for geometry work, and
   `Glyph.outline` is the same rings as an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) of *real cubics* for drawing.
 - [`TextLayout`](graphics.md#typography-kt-textlayout) — glyphs placed on baselines by AWT's own advances and kerning, plus tracking,
   multi-line and alignment. Every glyph in it is a [`PlacedGlyph`](graphics.md#typography-kt-placedglyph) carrying **mutable transform
   handles** (offset, rotation, scale, pivot). Those handles are how you animate letters
   individually, and `TextLayout.onCurve` is nothing but a routine that sets them from an
   [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline)'s arc length.

### Text space

Glyph and layout coordinates are **x right, y down**, origin at the first baseline, units = the
typeface's size in points. That is AWT's own glyph frame and it is also the frame Field's 2D
outputs use (`Rect`'s y grows downwards), so text handed straight to `Box.lines` or
`Box.showText` reads the right way up with no transform. The 3D bridges in `typography_field.kt`
flip y at their own boundary, because a mesh wants y up.

### The winding convention

A glyph's counter — the hole in `o`, `e`, `a`, `B` — is only a hole if something says so, and what
the font shipped is not enough to go on. (`isoContourFLines` in `contours.kt` leaves winding
arbitrary, and every consumer downstream has to cope.) So this file *decides*:

> For a ring `p0..pn`, signed area is `½Σ(xᵢyᵢ₊₁ − xᵢ₊₁yᵢ)` in text space. **Outer contours are
> positive; holes are negative.** A ring's `GlyphContour.depth` — how many other rings of the same
> glyph contain it — is authoritative: even depth is an outer contour, odd depth is a hole. A ring
> whose area sign disagrees with its depth is *reversed* on the way out.

Both representations obey it, so `contours.filter { it.isHole }` and the subpaths of
`Glyph.outline` agree, and `TypographyTest` asserts it on glyphs whose answer is known by eye
(`o` has one hole, `l` has none, `%` has two).

### AWT and the main run loop

`imaging_field.kt:417` explains why `montage` captions with a bitmap table instead of
`Graphics2D.drawString`: on macOS, touching the AWT font manager pulls in AppKit, which competes
with GLFW for the main run loop, and `Server.main` never initialises the toolkit. This
family cannot avoid the font manager — it *is* the font manager — so it contains the hazard in one
place, `Typefaces.warm`, whose KDoc carries the measured stack trace and the conclusion:

> **A JVM that wants glyph outlines and passes `-XstartOnFirstThread` must also pass
> `-Djava.awt.headless=true`.** Otherwise `CFontManager.loadFonts` dispatches to the process's first
> thread and waits forever for a run loop nobody is pumping.

`Typefaces.warm` detects that in four seconds and throws with that sentence in it, rather than
hanging the editor. Every jvm-main gallery in the tree already sets the property in the first line
of `main`, `jvmTest` does not need it (Gradle's test JVM has no `-XstartOnFirstThread`), and an
interactive Field window pumps its run loop through `glfwPollEvents` and so is expected to be
fine — expected, not tested; see `Typefaces.warm`. Everything after that one touch is pure
computation over cached outlines.

## typography_field.kt { #typography-field-kt }

The bridges out of a [`TextLayout`](graphics.md#typography-kt-textlayout) and into the four families Field already has.

`typography.kt` answers with *structure* — rings, depths, advances, handles — and structure is not
yet a drawing, a mesh, an image or a point cloud. This file is the missing hop, and it is the
reason the typography family is worth having at all: once a string is contours, letters get to be
inputs to machinery that never knew about text.

It is the typographic counterpart of `spatial_field.kt` (plane geometry → `FLine`) and
`mesh_field.kt` (`TriMesh` → `FLine`), and it is written to the same rule: every function here
returns a *value* — no `Box`, no output — except the two figure helpers at the bottom, which are
`drawToSVG` and so work headless, in a test and in the docs build.

Five bridges:

 1. **→ [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline)** (`TextLayout.toFLines`, `TextLayout.toFLine`, `Glyph.toFLine`). One line per
    glyph, so a per-glyph handle actually moves something, with the font's real cubics intact.
    Filling works because of `typography.kt`'s winding convention and nothing else: Skia and
    Java2D both fill non-zero, so a counter is a hole precisely because its ring runs the other
    way. `TextLayout.toFLines` takes `honourHoles = false` to show you the blob you get without a
    convention, which is the control arm the docs figure uses.
 2. **→ [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh)** (`TextLayout.toMesh`). Hole-aware extrusion: `extrudeMesh` in
    `mesh_generate.kt:619` and `triangulatePolygon` (`:547`) explicitly cannot do holes, so the
    caps here go through `FloatEarcut` with hole indices and the walls are emitted ring by ring
    from the *same* flattened vertices, which is what makes the result watertight — and makes an
    extruded `o` genus 1 and an extruded `l` genus 0.
 3. **→ an SDF** (`TextLayout.toSdf`). A 2D signed-distance grid, bilinearly sampled and extruded
    in z, so letters compose with `sdfSphere`, `sdfSmoothUnion`, `.twisted()` and everything else
    in `mesh_sdf.kt`, and `marchingCubes` will mesh the result.
 4. **→ [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img)** (`rasterizeText`). An analytic even-odd scanline fill of the layout's own rings —
    *not* `Graphics2D.drawString`, both because AWT text rendering in-process is what
    `imaging_field.kt:417` forbids and because filling our own outlines means a legible PNG is
    evidence about *this* code rather than about AWT's rasteriser.
 5. **→ points** (`TextLayout.samplePoints`, `TextLayout.toPointFLine`). Even-by-arc-length
    samples along the outlines, which is what the alife agents, the clusterers and the
    contourers in `clustering.kt` / `alife_agents.kt` consume.

Frames: bridges 1, 3, 4 and 5 stay in text space (y **down**, origin on the first baseline);
bridge 2 flips y at its boundary, because a mesh wants y up, and re-normalises winding when it
does.

### VertexBuffer { #vbuffer-kt-vertexbuffer }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">VertexBuffer</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">renderer</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Renderer</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">size</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">usage</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">VK10</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">VK&#95;BUFFER&#95;USAGE&#95;VERTEX&#95;BUFFER&#95;BIT</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">createCPU</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">HasBuffer</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">BufferWriteable</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/VBuffer/#L22)

this is, as far as I can tell, completely decoy — with resizable BAR (or unified memory on Apple Silicon) this staging buffer thing is just excess engineering _and_ writing shaders that do their own pulling is better _and_ device pointers set through push constants is faster and architecturally skips all of the descriptor nonsense

## StackSLBox.kt { #stackslbox-kt }

Host-side entry points for StackSL: compiling the stack language to GLSL, and evaluating it on
the GPU sample by sample. The language, its compiler and its diagnostics live in
`afield.lang.stacksl`; this file is the Kotlin surface a box calls.

`stackSL` holds a box's StackSL source, falling back to a parent box's. `compileStackSL`,
`stackSLToGlsl` and the standalone `slGlsl` are pure compilation and need no device. `slEval` and
`slSweep` actually run the compiled function: they wrap it in a small compute shader and dispatch
it through a `Renderer` that defaults to `fromContext()`, so they need a live graphics context.
Neither binds any texture sampler, so a source that needs one is rejected.

`slSweep` returns a [`StackSLSweep`](graphics.md#stackslbox-kt-stackslsweep), which implements `ToHTML` and draws itself as an inline SVG
plot of the four output channels with per-channel min/median/max; `StackSLSweep.h` is that HTML.

This only fills in after it, for a live slot: a block the generic carry had nothing for is seeded whole; a carried block gets, for each number it left without a value or binding, what was set on the slot or its literal. Nothing the generic carry put there is overwritten. |

## modelling.kt { #modelling-kt }

A self-tuning controller for pushing the *distribution* of a scalar signal towards a target
shape. You hand `AdaptiveDistributionController.pushSamples` a batch of samples each frame and it
returns a [`ControlOutput`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-controloutput) whose `appliedParams` are the next parameter values to send to whatever
produced them — a shader, a simulation, a tone curve.

The error signal comes from a [`FeatureExtractor`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-featureextractor); [`UniformQuantileFeatureExtractor`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-uniformquantilefeatureextractor) is the
built-in one and measures how far a set of sample quantiles sit from their targets. Internally
each feature gets a recursive-least-squares row (with forgetting) that learns a local Jacobian,
the step is a Tikhonov-regularised Gauss-Newton solve scaled by a confidence estimate, then
softened near the parameter bounds, rate-limited by `maxStep`, clipped, and finally offset by a
per-parameter sinusoidal dither so the estimator keeps seeing excitation.

`ControllerConfig.observationDelayFrames` is the important knob: it models pipeline latency
explicitly by pairing each observation with the command issued that many pushes earlier, so the
loop does not have to be slowed down to learn correctly. Use [`AdaptiveDistributionControllerBank`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-adaptivedistributioncontrollerbank)
for one controller per scene, and [`AdaptiveDistributionLoop`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-adaptivedistributionloop) to drive `observe`/`apply` from a
`Runloop` hook.

This is plain `DoubleArray` math with no GPU or `Box` dependency; every array in
[`ControllerConfig`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-controllerconfig) must be `parameterNames.size` long. `main` runs a synthetic drifting-Gaussian
plant against the controller and prints a trace.

## quantilewarp.kt { #quantilewarp-kt }

Reshapes a scalar signal's distribution by fitting a monotone 8-knot PCHIP curve from the
measured quantiles of recent samples onto the quantiles of a chosen target distribution —
`TargetDistributions.UnitNormal` by default, or any [`QuantileFunction`](graphics.md#quantilewarp-kt-quantilefunction).

`AdaptiveQuantileWarp.update` takes a batch of samples, merges it with the last
`historyFrames` batches, and returns a [`QuantileWarpState`](graphics.md#quantilewarp-kt-quantilewarpstate): the knot pairs, an
`QuantileWarpState.evaluate` for CPU-side use, and the same 16 knots packed into four `vec4`s
ready for push constants via `QuantileWarpState.applyToPushConstants`. Successive states are
smoothed towards each other by `smoothingAlpha` and forced strictly increasing, so the curve
stays invertible even when the input degenerates.

`fieldQuantileWarpIncludeSource` is the matching GLSL — `fieldQuantileWarp8` and
`fieldQuantileWarpMix` evaluate the identical PCHIP curve on the GPU — and is reachable from
shader source as the built-in include named by `FIELD_QUANTILE_WARP_INCLUDE_NAME`.
`Box.fieldProbeQuantileWarp` closes the loop: it installs a runloop hook that drains a
`ShaderFieldProbe`, updates the warp, calls your `apply` callback and renders a knot table into a
box display channel.

Two constraints: exactly eight strictly increasing probabilities inside `(0, 1)`, and
`Box.fieldProbeQuantileWarp` needs a live `Box` plus a probe configured for continuous snapshot
reads.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/statistics/quantilewarp.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/statistics/quantilewarp/)

**Used in:** [Measuring dependence between two signals](../statistics_examples.md), [Field 4 Graphics](../afield_four_graphics.md)

## FLineInspect.kt { #flineinspect-kt }

Make a figure answerable: `inspect` draws FLines the way `lines` does and then *names* whatever you
click on, in the figure's own coordinates.

The problem it solves is the one the panel documents ran into — a figure was drawn, and then the
numbers about it were fished back out with `println` because there was no way to ask the picture
"which edge is this, and how far along it am I?". `inspect` wires `FLine.onClick` and
`FLine.hoverColor` for every line it is given, so a click reports the element under the pointer
(see [`FLineIntersection`](graphics.md#standarddrawing-kt-flineintersection)) and writes a readable card into a second output channel.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/FLineInspect.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/visualization/FLineInspect/)

## pointing_render.kt { #pointing-render-kt }

Seeing what the pointer found: the picked part lit, a crosshair where the pointer was aimed, and a
caption that names what it hit.

### Why this is in the layer and not left to the caller

Because "it compiles" and "a hit record came back non-null" are both worthless as evidence for
something whose whole job is to tell a person what they are touching. The failure mode is not a
crash; it is *the wrong part lit*, or a pointer that is confidently off by the height of a caption
band. Neither shows up in a unit test's return value, and both are obvious in a picture.

So the layer ships its own way of drawing itself, `SpatialPointerPixelTest` decodes the PNG back
out and reads samples from it, and the demo transcript uses the same call a person would.

### What the picture is

`TriMesh.renderPng`'s rasterizer, over a mesh whose per-vertex colours have been repainted by part
(`TriMesh.coloredByPart`), with a crosshair composited on afterwards at the pointer's pixel. All of
it CPU: no GPU, no window, no AWT — so it runs inside a live Field box, inside a test, and inside a
headless docs capture, identically.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val scene = pickScene { add("model", mesh, parts = builder.groups()) }
val camera = MeshView().rayCamera(scene.mergedMesh())
val at = Vec2(360f, 270f)
display(scene.pointerFigureHtml(camera, at))
```

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/pointing_render.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/visualization/pointing_render/)
